text: The Sun delivers more energy to Earth in one hour than humanity uses in an entire year. This extraordinary abundance makes solar power one of the most promising long-term energy sources.

Solar photovoltaic capacity has grown from virtually nothing in 2000 to over 1,400 gigawatts globally by 2023, making it the fastest-growing energy technology in history. Costs have fallen by more than 90% over the same period.

The Bhadla Solar Park in India is the world's largest solar farm, covering over 14,000 acres in the Thar Desert with an installed capacity of 2,245 megawatts. It powers millions of homes and cost approximately $1.4 billion to build.

Wind energy currently supplies around 7% of global electricity generation, with total installed capacity exceeding 900 gigawatts worldwide as of 2023. China, the United States, and Germany are the three largest wind power producers.

The Gansu Wind Farm in China, also known as the Jiuquan Wind Power Base, is the world's largest wind farm with a planned capacity of 20,000 megawatts — enough to power tens of millions of homes. It is located in the Gobi Desert.

Offshore wind turbines can be significantly larger than onshore models; the latest designs stand over 260 meters tall with rotor diameters exceeding 220 meters. A single rotation of such a turbine's blade can generate enough electricity to power a home for a day.

Hydropower is the world's largest source of renewable electricity, generating about 16% of global electricity and more than 60% of all renewable electricity. It has been in commercial use for over 130 years.

The Three Gorges Dam in China is the world's largest hydropower station, with an installed capacity of 22,500 megawatts. Built across the Yangtze River, it required the relocation of over 1.3 million people during construction.

Norway generates approximately 90% of its electricity from hydropower, making it one of the most renewable power systems in the world. The country's numerous fjords and rivers provide exceptional conditions for hydroelectric generation.

source.name: Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate

text: Nuclear power plants currently supply about 10% of global electricity from around 440 operating reactors in 32 countries. France relies most heavily on nuclear energy, with it providing roughly 70% of the country's electricity.

A single uranium fuel pellet — about the size of a fingertip — contains as much energy as 17,000 cubic feet of natural gas, 1,780 pounds of coal, or 149 gallons of oil. This extraordinary energy density is a key advantage of nuclear fission.

The Chernobyl disaster of 1986 and the Fukushima Daiichi accident of 2011 are the only two nuclear accidents rated at the maximum Level 7 on the International Nuclear Event Scale. Both events led to widespread evacuations and long-term radiological contamination.

Geothermal energy harnesses heat from within the Earth and currently provides electricity to about 90 million people worldwide. Iceland meets nearly 100% of its heating needs and about 70% of its total primary energy from geothermal and hydropower sources.

The Geysers in California is the world's largest geothermal complex, with a generating capacity of about 900 megawatts — enough power for a city the size of San Francisco. The site has been producing electricity since 1960.

Coal was the dominant fuel of the Industrial Revolution and powered the steam engines that transformed manufacturing, transportation, and society throughout the 18th and 19th centuries. It remains the world's largest single source of electricity generation today.

Coal burning generates more CO2 per unit of energy than any other fossil fuel, emitting roughly 820 grams of CO2 per kilowatt-hour of electricity produced. Natural gas emits about half as much, while renewables produce near-zero operational emissions.

China is by far the world's largest coal consumer, accounting for over half of global coal consumption. The country has pledged to peak coal use before 2025 and achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 as part of its climate commitments.

Oil was first commercially drilled in Titusville, Pennsylvania, in 1859 by Edwin Drake, marking the beginning of the modern petroleum industry. Within decades, oil had become the world's most traded commodity and a cornerstone of industrial civilization.

The world consumes approximately 100 million barrels of oil every day, used primarily for transportation fuels, plastics, and petrochemicals. The United States, China, and India are the three largest oil-consuming nations.

Saudi Arabia holds the world's second-largest proven oil reserves at about 268 billion barrels, behind Venezuela's 303 billion barrels. Together, the five OPEC nations with the largest reserves hold more than 70% of the world's total proven oil supply.

OPEC, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, was founded in Baghdad in September 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela. It was created to coordinate oil production and pricing policies among major oil-exporting nations.

The 1973 OPEC oil embargo, triggered by Arab members in response to U.S. support for Israel during the Yom Kippur War, caused oil prices to quadruple in just a few months. The crisis led to widespread fuel shortages, long lines at gas stations, and spurred significant investment in energy alternatives.

Natural gas is the cleanest-burning fossil fuel, producing about 50% less CO2 than coal when used to generate electricity. It has become a dominant transitional fuel as countries move away from coal while expanding renewable energy infrastructure.

Russia holds the world's largest proven natural gas reserves, with approximately 37.4 trillion cubic meters — enough to supply the entire world's gas needs for roughly a decade. The country is also one of the world's top gas exporters.

Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) is natural gas cooled to -162°C, shrinking its volume by about 600 times to allow ocean transport in special tanker ships. The global LNG trade has grown enormously, allowing gas to be shipped between continents like oil.

Green hydrogen is produced by using renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen through electrolysis, emitting no greenhouse gases in the process. It is considered one of the most promising fuels for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors like steelmaking, shipping, and aviation.

Today, over 95% of the world's hydrogen is produced from fossil fuels — primarily natural gas through a process called steam methane reforming — making it 'grey hydrogen.' This process releases significant CO2 unless combined with carbon capture.

Biofuels are transportation fuels derived from living materials such as corn, sugarcane, soybeans, or wood. Brazil and the United States together account for more than 80% of global biofuel production, with Brazil pioneering ethanol from sugarcane as far back as the 1970s.

Tidal energy exploits the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun on ocean waters to generate predictable, reliable electricity. The world's first large-scale tidal power station, the 240-megawatt La Rance barrage in France, has operated since 1966.

The Bay of Fundy in Canada experiences the world's highest tidal range, with water levels rising and falling up to 17 meters (56 feet) during each tidal cycle. This makes it one of the most promising sites for tidal energy development in the world.

Lithium-ion batteries, which power everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and grid-scale storage, have seen their cost fall by over 97% since they were first commercialized in the early 1990s. This dramatic cost reduction has transformed both mobility and energy storage.

The world's largest battery energy storage system, as of 2024, is the Moss Landing Energy Storage Facility in California with a capacity of about 1,200 megawatt-hours. Grid-scale battery storage is being deployed rapidly to balance intermittent renewable energy sources.

Pumped-storage hydropower is the world's most widely used form of large-scale energy storage, accounting for over 90% of global storage capacity. It works by pumping water uphill during periods of low demand and releasing it through turbines when demand peaks.

The world's first public electricity supply was established by Thomas Edison in 1882 in New York City, powering 59 customers from the Pearl Street Station. The station used direct current (DC) generators — a technology that would soon be challenged by Nikola Tesla's alternating current (AC) system.

The 'War of Currents' in the late 19th century was a fierce competition between Thomas Edison's direct current (DC) and Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse's alternating current (AC). AC eventually won because it could be transmitted efficiently over long distances using transformers.

Global electricity demand is expected to nearly triple by 2050, driven primarily by the electrification of transport, heating, and industry as the world decarbonizes. Meeting this demand while cutting emissions is one of the central challenges of the energy transition.

Energy efficiency is often called the 'first fuel' because saving energy through efficiency measures is frequently cheaper than producing new energy. The IEA estimates that doubling the global rate of energy efficiency improvement could deliver about 40% of the emissions reductions needed by 2040.

LED lighting is up to 90% more energy-efficient than traditional incandescent bulbs and lasts 25 times longer. The global shift to LED lighting has already saved enormous amounts of electricity and is one of the most cost-effective energy efficiency improvements available.

Buildings account for approximately 40% of global energy consumption and about 33% of CO2 emissions when including construction. Improving building insulation, windows, and heating systems is one of the most impactful strategies for reducing energy use.

Global primary energy consumption reached approximately 580 exajoules in 2022, with fossil fuels still supplying about 80% of the world's energy. An exajoule equals one quintillion joules — roughly the energy content of 170 million barrels of oil.

source.name: BP Statistical Review of World Energy

text: The United States is the world's largest energy consumer on a per capita basis among major economies, consuming roughly twice the energy per person as the European Union. American energy intensity has fallen significantly since the 1970s due to efficiency improvements.

Approximately 733 million people — about 9% of the world's population — still lack access to electricity as of 2023, with the majority living in Sub-Saharan Africa. Energy poverty is closely linked to poverty, poor health outcomes, and limited economic opportunity.

About 2.3 billion people worldwide still cook using open fires or inefficient stoves fueled by wood, charcoal, coal, or dung, causing indoor air pollution that kills an estimated 3.2 million people each year — more than malaria. Clean cooking access is a major component of the UN's Sustainable Development Goal 7.

The global energy transition refers to the ongoing shift from fossil fuel-dominated energy systems to low-carbon sources, primarily renewables. The IEA's Net Zero by 2050 scenario requires that no new oil, gas, or coal development projects be approved beyond those already committed.

Renewable energy sources — including solar, wind, hydro, and others — now account for about 30% of global electricity generation as of 2023, up from just 19% in 2010. Solar and wind together are the fastest-growing electricity sources in history.

Nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun, could theoretically provide nearly limitless clean energy. In December 2022, the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory achieved ignition for the first time — producing more fusion energy than the laser energy delivered to the target.

ITER, the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor being built in France, is the world's largest fusion experiment and involves 35 nations. It is designed to demonstrate that fusion can produce ten times more energy than it consumes, with first plasma expected in the late 2020s.

A smart grid uses digital communications and sensors to detect and react to local changes in electricity supply and demand in real time. Smart grids can reduce energy waste, integrate more renewable energy, and allow consumers to manage their electricity use more efficiently.

The United States power grid is actually three large interconnected systems — the Eastern Interconnection, the Western Interconnection, and the Texas Interconnection (ERCOT). Texas deliberately keeps its grid separate from the others to avoid federal regulation.

The Northeast blackout of 2003 was one of the largest power outages in North American history, affecting 55 million people across the northeastern United States and Canada. It was triggered by a software bug and cascaded across interconnected power lines, costing an estimated $6 billion.

High-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines can carry electricity over thousands of kilometers with much lower energy losses than conventional alternating current lines. China operates the world's longest HVDC lines, including the 3,284-km Changji–Guquan link.

The global capacity of installed solar panels doubles roughly every three years, a pattern sometimes called 'Swanson's Law,' analogous to Moore's Law in computing. This exponential growth has caught most energy forecasters by surprise.

Perovskite solar cells are an emerging photovoltaic technology that has rapidly improved in efficiency from 3.8% in 2009 to over 26% in laboratory settings by 2024. They could eventually be printed onto flexible surfaces at very low cost, potentially revolutionizing solar power.

Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants use mirrors or lenses to focus sunlight onto a receiver, generating heat that drives a turbine. Unlike PV panels, CSP can store heat in molten salt to generate electricity even when the sun isn't shining.

The wind industry's capacity factor — the percentage of time a turbine generates at full power — has improved dramatically, with modern offshore turbines achieving capacity factors above 50%. This means offshore wind is now producing electricity more than half the time at maximum output.

Denmark was the first country to install offshore wind turbines at commercial scale, beginning in 1991. Today, Denmark generates roughly 50% of its total electricity from wind power — one of the highest proportions in the world.

Shale oil and gas production, enabled by hydraulic fracturing (fracking) and horizontal drilling, transformed the United States into the world's largest oil and natural gas producer by the mid-2010s. The shale revolution reshaped global energy markets and significantly reduced U.S. dependence on imported oil.

The energy return on investment (EROI) for oil was once as high as 100:1, meaning 100 units of energy were obtained for every 1 unit invested in extraction. Today, as easy reserves are depleted, the global average EROI for oil has fallen to around 15:1, making production progressively more energy-intensive.

Electric vehicles (EVs) are significantly more energy-efficient than internal combustion engine vehicles, converting about 85–90% of electrical energy to motion versus 17–21% for gasoline engines. This efficiency advantage makes EVs cheaper to run even if electricity is generated partly from fossil fuels.

Global EV sales surpassed 10 million for the first time in 2022 and reached 14 million in 2023, representing roughly 18% of all new cars sold worldwide. China leads in both EV production and sales, accounting for about 60% of the global total.

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System, completed in 1977, stretches 800 miles (1,287 km) from Prudhoe Bay to the port of Valdez and has transported over 18 billion barrels of oil. It was built to withstand extreme cold, permafrost, and earthquake activity.

Natural gas power plants that use combined-cycle technology — running exhaust heat through a steam turbine in addition to the gas turbine — can achieve efficiency rates of up to 62%. This is roughly double the efficiency of a conventional coal plant.

The Itaipu Dam on the Brazil-Paraguay border was the world's largest hydropower plant by capacity for many years, generating enough electricity to supply 90% of Paraguay's and 17% of Brazil's total electricity needs. It remains one of the most productive power plants in the world.

Wave energy, which harnesses the kinetic energy of ocean surface waves, is still largely in the research and development stage but holds enormous theoretical potential. The global wave energy resource is estimated at over 2,000 terawatt-hours per year.

Solid-state batteries, which replace the liquid electrolyte of conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid material, could offer higher energy density, faster charging, and improved safety. Many automakers and researchers believe they represent the next major leap in battery technology.

Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolyte solutions held in external tanks, allowing their capacity to be increased simply by using larger tanks. They are particularly suited for long-duration grid storage of 4 to 12 hours and are increasingly used alongside renewable energy installations.

Biomass — organic material from plants and animals — is the oldest energy source used by humans, going back to the first use of fire. Today, modern biomass provides about 10% of global primary energy and is the largest single source of renewable energy when traditional uses like wood burning are included.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology captures CO2 from power plants or industrial facilities and stores it underground in geological formations. The IEA considers CCS essential for achieving global net-zero emissions, particularly for hard-to-abate industrial sectors.

The Sleipner gas field in Norway has been injecting CO2 into a saline aquifer beneath the North Sea since 1996, making it one of the world's first and longest-running commercial-scale carbon capture and storage projects. It stores about 1 million tonnes of CO2 per year.

The global energy industry — including fuel production, electricity generation, and energy equipment — employs approximately 67 million people worldwide, according to IRENA's 2023 Renewable Energy and Jobs report. The renewable energy sector alone employed 13.7 million people globally in 2022.

The first nuclear power plant to generate electricity for a national grid was the Obninsk Nuclear Power Plant in the Soviet Union, which began operating in June 1954. It had a modest capacity of just 5 megawatts but proved the commercial viability of nuclear energy.

Small modular reactors (SMRs) are nuclear reactors with a capacity of less than 300 megawatts that can be factory-built and shipped to sites. They are seen as a way to make nuclear energy faster to deploy, more flexible, and potentially cheaper than conventional large reactors.

The amount of energy consumed by data centers worldwide is estimated at 200–250 terawatt-hours annually as of 2022, roughly equal to the electricity consumption of a medium-sized country like Argentina. With AI driving rapid data center expansion, this figure is expected to rise sharply.

Vampire power, or standby power consumption, refers to the electricity used by electronic devices while they are switched off or in standby mode. Studies estimate it accounts for 5–10% of residential electricity consumption in developed countries.

The world's first commercial wind farm was established at Crotched Mountain in New Hampshire, USA, in 1980, with a modest capacity of just 0.6 megawatts. Wind energy has since grown to become one of the world's leading electricity sources.

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential approximately 80 times greater than CO2 over a 20-year period. Natural gas is primarily methane, and leaks along the supply chain — known as fugitive emissions — significantly undermine the climate benefits of gas over coal.

The world's largest oil spill occurred during the Gulf War in 1991, when Iraqi forces deliberately opened oil valves and set fire to Kuwaiti oil wells, releasing an estimated 4–8 million barrels of oil into the Persian Gulf. The resulting environmental damage took years to remediate.

Thermal coal and metallurgical coal serve different purposes: thermal coal is burned for electricity generation, while metallurgical (coking) coal is used in steelmaking. Metallurgical coal is much harder to replace with alternatives because steel production requires carbon as a chemical reducing agent, not just as a heat source.

The concept of peak oil — the idea that global oil production would eventually reach a maximum and irreversibly decline — was first proposed by geophysicist M. King Hubbert in 1956. While Hubbert correctly predicted U.S. oil production would peak around 1970, global peak oil predictions have repeatedly been revised due to new technology and discoveries.

Electricity transmission losses — the energy lost as heat when current flows through power lines — average around 8–15% in most countries. High-voltage transmission reduces these losses dramatically, which is why power is stepped up to high voltages before long-distance transmission and stepped back down near consumers.

The global average levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) from new utility-scale solar PV fell below $0.05 per kilowatt-hour in 2022, making it cheaper than any fossil fuel power source. The LCOE for onshore wind also fell below $0.05/kWh, making these the cheapest electricity sources ever recorded.

Heat pumps are one of the most efficient ways to heat and cool buildings, moving heat rather than generating it and delivering 2–4 units of heat energy for every unit of electrical energy consumed. They can work in reverse for cooling and are rapidly replacing gas boilers in many countries.

The Hoover Dam, completed in 1936 on the Colorado River between Nevada and Arizona, was once the world's largest hydroelectric facility and remains one of America's most iconic engineering achievements. It has a capacity of about 2,080 megawatts and provides power to Nevada, Arizona, and California.

Run-of-river hydropower plants generate electricity from the natural flow of a river without requiring a large reservoir, making them less disruptive to ecosystems than large dams. They are increasingly favored for new hydro development due to their lower environmental and social impacts.

Approximately 84% of global final energy consumption in the transportation sector is still met by oil. Electrifying transport is thus one of the most impactful ways to reduce both oil demand and greenhouse gas emissions.

The global installed capacity of renewable energy surpassed that of coal for the first time in 2023, according to IRENA, marking a historic milestone. Solar alone added a record 345 gigawatts of new capacity that year — more than any other energy source in history.

Agrivoltaics is the practice of co-locating solar panels and agriculture on the same land, allowing crops to grow in the shade beneath or between panels. Studies show this dual land use can improve crop yields in hot climates (by reducing heat stress) and increase land productivity by up to 70%.

The energy sector is the source of about 73% of all human-caused greenhouse gas emissions globally. Transforming this sector through decarbonization is therefore the single most important step in addressing climate change.

The Atacama Desert in Chile is considered the best location in the world for solar energy generation, with some sites receiving up to 9.5 kilowatt-hours of solar irradiance per square meter per day. For comparison, cloudy northern Europe receives only about 2–3 kWh/m²/day.

Space-based solar power involves placing giant solar panels in geostationary orbit to collect sunlight 24 hours a day, then beaming energy back to Earth as microwaves. While still conceptual, it has attracted serious investment from national space agencies including those of the U.S., Europe, Japan, and China.

Geothermal 'hot dry rock' or enhanced geothermal systems (EGS) drill deep into the Earth's crust and inject water to create artificial reservoirs of superheated steam. If commercialized, EGS could access geothermal energy virtually anywhere on Earth, not just volcanic regions.

The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, aims to limit global average temperature increases to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, with efforts to stay within 1.5°C. It calls on all countries to submit national climate pledges, known as Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), and ratchet up ambition over time.

source.name: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change

text: The grid parity tipping point — when the cost of generating electricity from renewables equals or is less than conventional sources — has been reached by solar and wind in most of the world. In many sunbelt countries, new solar power is now the cheapest form of electricity ever built.

Japan's Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident in March 2011, triggered by the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, led to the shutdown of almost all of Japan's nuclear plants. Japan subsequently turned to fossil fuel imports at great cost, and its CO2 emissions rose significantly in the years following.

Thorium is a radioactive element that could be used as nuclear fuel and is three to four times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium. Thorium-fueled reactors produce less long-lived radioactive waste than uranium reactors and cannot be used to make nuclear weapons, making it attractive as a future fuel.

The world's oil tanker fleet transports roughly two billion tonnes of crude oil and petroleum products annually, making it one of the largest components of global shipping. The largest supertankers (VLCCs) can carry over 2 million barrels of oil in a single voyage.

Germany's Energiewende ('energy turn') policy, launched in 2000, aimed to transition the country from nuclear and fossil fuels to renewables. Germany has achieved over 50% renewable electricity generation but has also struggled with high consumer electricity prices and grid stability challenges.

source.name: Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Climate Action

text: Compressed air energy storage (CAES) stores energy by compressing air underground in caverns or depleted gas fields, then releasing it through turbines to generate electricity. It is one of the few large-scale, long-duration storage technologies that can store energy for days or weeks.

Power-to-gas technology uses surplus renewable electricity to produce hydrogen via electrolysis, which can then be converted to synthetic methane and injected into existing gas pipelines. This offers a way to store large amounts of renewable energy using existing gas infrastructure.

Oil palm plantations used for biofuel production have been linked to deforestation in Indonesia and Malaysia, raising serious questions about the sustainability of certain biofuels. When forest and peatland clearing is accounted for, palm oil-based biofuels can have a much higher carbon footprint than the diesel they replace.

The Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman, is the world's most important oil chokepoint — roughly 21 million barrels of oil pass through it daily, representing about 20% of global oil trade. Any disruption here would immediately impact world energy markets.

The first offshore oil well was drilled in 1897 off the coast of Summerland, California, extending from a pier into the Pacific Ocean. Today, offshore oil and gas production accounts for about 30% of global output, with wells operating in waters several kilometers deep.

Photovoltaic solar cells work on the photovoltaic effect, first observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839 when he noticed that certain materials produced an electric current when exposed to light. The first practical silicon solar cell was built at Bell Labs in 1954 with an efficiency of just 6%.

Global coal reserves are estimated at about 1.07 trillion tonnes — enough to last roughly 130 years at current consumption rates. However, burning all known coal reserves would push global temperatures far above the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C target.

The Drake Well in Titusville, Pennsylvania, which struck oil in 1859 at just 69 feet deep, triggered the world's first oil boom. Thousands of speculators and drillers flooded into western Pennsylvania, establishing the template for oil rushes that would follow worldwide.

Approximately 40% of global electricity is still generated from coal as of 2023. While coal's share of electricity is falling in Europe and North America, demand continues to grow in parts of Asia, particularly India, which is rapidly expanding coal-fired generation to meet surging electricity demand.

The concept of net metering allows homeowners with rooftop solar panels to sell excess electricity back to the grid, receiving credits on their utility bills. This policy has been instrumental in driving residential solar adoption in the United States and other countries.

Wind turbines require a minimum wind speed of about 3–4 meters per second (7–9 mph) to start generating power and reach maximum output at around 12–14 m/s. They automatically shut down in very high winds above 25 m/s to prevent structural damage.

Texas is the leading U.S. state for both wind and solar energy generation, producing more wind power than any other state and rapidly expanding utility-scale solar. Texas also leads the nation in total electricity generation from all sources.

Hydrogen fuel cells generate electricity through an electrochemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, producing only water as a byproduct. Fuel cell technology powers some buses, trains, and forklifts today and is being explored for long-haul trucking and shipping.

The world's first tidal stream generator connected to a national grid was SeaGen, installed in Strangford Lough in Northern Ireland in 2008. It had a capacity of 1.2 megawatts and operated successfully for years, paving the way for commercial tidal stream development.

Carbon pricing — through taxes or cap-and-trade systems — puts a direct price on CO2 emissions, making fossil fuels more expensive and creating economic incentives to switch to cleaner energy. As of 2023, carbon pricing schemes cover about 23% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Sub-Saharan Africa has some of the world's best solar and wind resources yet paradoxically has the lowest renewable energy investment per capita. The continent generates less electricity in total than Germany alone, despite having 15 times the population.

The Blue Dune project in the Netherlands demonstrated that offshore wind turbines can be designed to create artificial reefs and marine habitat at their bases, turning energy infrastructure into marine biodiversity hotspots. Wind turbine foundations have been shown to increase fish populations in surrounding waters.

The sodium-sulfur (NaS) battery operates at high temperatures around 300°C and is used primarily for large-scale grid energy storage. Japan has been a leader in deploying NaS batteries for grid stabilization, with Tokyo Electric Power Company operating some of the world's largest installations.

The oil price collapse of 1986, caused by Saudi Arabia dramatically increasing production to reclaim market share, saw prices fall from over $30 per barrel to below $10. This price shock devastated oil-dependent economies and contributed to the economic difficulties of the Soviet Union.

Nuclear power plants generate very low lifecycle carbon emissions — about 12 grams of CO2 per kilowatt-hour — comparable to wind and solar. This makes nuclear one of the cleanest electricity sources available in terms of greenhouse gas emissions.

The world's deepest oil well, the Sakhalin-I Odoptu OP-11 well drilled in 2011 off Russia's Sakhalin Island, extended 12.345 kilometers (7.67 miles) horizontally — making it the longest extended-reach well ever drilled at that time. Modern directional drilling allows oil companies to reach reservoirs far from the surface drilling point.

Demand response programs allow utilities to pay large electricity consumers — factories, data centers, commercial buildings — to temporarily reduce their load during peak demand periods. This flexibility can defer the need for expensive new power plants and help integrate more renewable energy.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) was established in 1974 in response to the 1973 oil crisis, initially as an energy security organization for oil-importing countries. It has since evolved into a leading global authority on all aspects of energy, tracking statistics and shaping energy policy.

Solar panel efficiency records are frequently broken; the highest ever achieved in a laboratory setting reached over 47% conversion efficiency using multi-junction concentrator cells. Commercial panels sold today typically achieve 20–23% efficiency, with premium models exceeding 24%.

A tokamak is the dominant design for experimental nuclear fusion reactors, using powerful magnetic fields to confine superheated plasma (over 100 million degrees Celsius — hotter than the Sun's core) in a doughnut-shaped chamber. The ITER tokamak will be the world's largest when completed.

Ancient Romans used geothermal hot springs for bathing and heating, and the Icelandic settlers of the 9th century used natural hot springs for cooking and washing. The first use of geothermal energy to generate electricity was in Larderello, Italy, in 1904.

The global average per capita energy consumption is about 80 gigajoules per year, but this masks huge disparities — the average American consumes nearly 300 GJ/year while the average Sub-Saharan African consumes less than 20 GJ/year. Bridging this gap while decarbonizing is a central challenge of sustainable development.

source.name: BP Statistical Review of World Energy

text: The concept of energy return on investment (EROI) for wind power is approximately 20:1 to 30:1, meaning modern wind turbines produce 20–30 times the energy used in their manufacture, installation, and decommissioning. This compares favorably with oil at around 15:1 and coal at around 30:1.

The Deepwater Horizon oil spill of 2010 in the Gulf of Mexico released approximately 4.9 million barrels of oil over 87 days, making it the largest accidental marine oil spill in history. The disaster killed 11 workers and caused devastating ecological damage across a vast area of the Gulf.

source.name: U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

text: The US Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 is the largest climate and clean energy investment in American history, committing approximately $369 billion to accelerate the energy transition. Economists estimate it will drive $3 trillion or more in clean energy investment over the following decade.

Floating solar panels installed on reservoirs, lakes, and irrigation ponds — known as floatovoltaics — can simultaneously generate electricity and reduce water evaporation. Studies show they can reduce evaporation by up to 70%, which is particularly valuable in water-stressed regions.

The global oil and gas industry receives an estimated $1 trillion or more in explicit and implicit subsidies annually, according to IMF calculations that include the uncounted cost of pollution and climate damage. Phasing out these subsidies is seen by economists as a key step in accelerating the clean energy transition.

Antarctica's Lake Untersee has been proposed as a model for what life might look like under the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn — but it's also relevant to geothermal energy research, as volcanic heat beneath ice sheets can create liquid water environments. Geothermal activity beneath the West Antarctic Ice Sheet could affect ice dynamics and sea level rise.

Cellulosic ethanol, produced from non-food plant material like agricultural waste, switchgrass, or wood chips, offers a more sustainable biofuel pathway than corn or sugar ethanol. However, the technology has been slower and more expensive to commercialize than initially projected.

The global average cost of offshore wind power fell by 60% between 2010 and 2020, from around $0.17/kWh to $0.084/kWh, driven by larger turbines, better installation methods, and project finance innovation. Further cost reductions are expected as the technology continues to mature.

Natural gas was initially considered a nuisance byproduct during early oil drilling and was simply burned off (flared) at the wellhead. Today, flaring still wastes about 140 billion cubic meters of gas per year globally — equivalent to the combined gas consumption of Central and South America.

source.name: World Bank Global Gas Flaring Reduction Partnership

text: The concept of the hydrogen economy envisions hydrogen as a universal clean energy carrier, stored, transported, and burned or used in fuel cells to power industry, transport, and heating. The IEA estimates global hydrogen demand could reach 530 million tonnes per year by 2050 in a net-zero scenario.

India is the world's third-largest energy consumer and has set an ambitious target of 500 gigawatts of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030 — nearly half its total projected power capacity. The country is simultaneously one of the fastest-growing renewable energy markets and one of the world's biggest coal consumers.

Virtual power plants (VPPs) aggregate thousands of distributed energy resources — rooftop solar, home batteries, EV chargers, smart appliances — and manage them collectively as if they were a single large power plant. They can respond to grid signals in milliseconds and are increasingly being used to provide grid stability services.

The Exxon Valdez oil spill in Alaska in 1989 released approximately 257,000 barrels of crude oil into Prince William Sound, coating 1,300 miles of coastline and killing hundreds of thousands of seabirds and marine mammals. It remains one of the most significant environmental disasters in U.S. history.

Uranium used in nuclear reactors must first be enriched — increasing the concentration of fissile U-235 from its natural 0.7% to about 3–5% for power reactors. Weapons-grade uranium is enriched to over 90%, which is why uranium enrichment is a sensitive proliferation concern in international diplomacy.

Power grids must maintain a precise balance between electricity supply and demand at all times — in most systems, frequency must stay within 0.5 Hz of 50 or 60 Hz. Deviations beyond safe limits can damage equipment and trigger cascading failures across entire networks.

The average American home uses about 10,500 kilowatt-hours of electricity per year, but this varies enormously by region — homes in the hot, humid Southeast use much more for air conditioning, while homes in the mild Pacific Northwest use far less. Space cooling accounts for the largest share of residential electricity use in many countries.

The sun's core fuses about 620 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second, releasing energy equivalent to 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts — a figure that dwarfs all human energy use by an incomprehensible margin. Only a tiny fraction of this energy, intercepted by Earth, sustains all life and human civilization.

The Alberta oil sands in Canada contain one of the world's largest deposits of oil — about 166 billion barrels of proven reserves. However, extracting oil from oil sands (also called tar sands) is energy-intensive and produces significantly more greenhouse gas emissions than conventional oil production.

The interconnection of national power grids across borders — such as the European transmission network — allows countries to trade electricity and balance renewable energy variability. The European grid spans 40 countries and is one of the world's most complex interconnected power systems.

source.name: European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity

text: Micro-hydropower systems — generating less than 100 kilowatts — can provide reliable, low-cost electricity to remote villages near streams and rivers, often without any grid connection. They have transformed energy access for millions of people in Nepal, Peru, and other mountainous developing countries.

The Soviet Union's gas pipeline to Europe, begun in the 1970s and expanded significantly thereafter, created deep energy interdependencies that shaped European geopolitics for decades. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and subsequent gas supply cuts forced Europe to rapidly accelerate its shift to renewables and LNG imports.

Biogas is produced by the anaerobic digestion of organic waste — sewage, animal manure, food scraps — and consists primarily of methane. It can be used directly as fuel or upgraded to 'biomethane' and injected into natural gas pipelines, providing a renewable substitute for fossil gas.

The global renewable energy auction market — where governments award long-term power purchase contracts to the cheapest bidder — has been a key driver of solar and wind cost reductions. Competitive auctions in countries like Chile, UAE, and India have repeatedly set new record-low prices for renewable electricity.

The world's first commercial geothermal power station was built at Larderello in Tuscany, Italy, in 1911, and the site still generates electricity today. Larderello remains one of the most productive geothermal facilities in Europe, with an installed capacity of approximately 800 megawatts.

Superconducting power cables carry electricity with almost zero resistance when cooled to extremely low temperatures, dramatically reducing transmission losses. While still expensive, superconducting cables are being piloted in dense urban grids where conventional cables cannot handle the required current density.

The world's oceans absorb about 90% of the extra heat trapped by greenhouse gases, and ocean thermal energy conversion (OTEC) exploits the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep water to generate electricity. OTEC plants can theoretically operate 24/7 as baseload power in tropical regions.

China's Belt and Road Initiative has financed billions of dollars of coal power plants in developing countries, though the government announced in 2021 it would no longer fund overseas coal projects. China is now the world's largest overseas financier of renewable energy infrastructure.

Passive house (Passivhaus) buildings are designed to maintain comfortable temperatures year-round with minimal active heating or cooling by using excellent insulation, airtight construction, and heat-recovery ventilation. A certified passive house uses up to 90% less heating energy than a conventional building.

The energy stored in all global uranium reserves is estimated to be far greater than that in all fossil fuels combined, even using today's once-through reactor technology. With advanced breeder reactors that can use spent fuel and depleted uranium, the resource base expands further still.

The Manhattan Project, which developed the first nuclear weapons during World War II, laid the scientific and engineering foundation for civilian nuclear power. Several of the physicists involved, including Enrico Fermi who achieved the first self-sustaining chain reaction in 1942, went on to shape the early nuclear energy industry.

source.name: U.S. Department of Energy Office of History

text: The global energy storage market — including batteries, pumped hydro, and other technologies — is projected by the IEA to need 10 times its current capacity by 2030 to support a net-zero energy system. Battery storage alone is expected to grow from about 30 GW in 2022 to over 1,500 GW by 2030.

The oil industry uses the unit 'barrel' (abbreviated bbl), equal to 42 U.S. gallons or about 159 liters. The barrel as a unit of oil measurement originated in the Pennsylvania oil fields of the 1860s, when 42-gallon wooden whiskey barrels were found to be the most practical containers.

Wind energy has a land area advantage over solar in cold climates because turbines can operate efficiently even when covered in snow, whereas panels must be cleared or tilted to shed snow accumulation. However, some turbine models require special cold-climate heating systems to prevent blade icing.

OPEC+ is an alliance between the 13 OPEC members and 10 additional major oil producers including Russia, Kazakhstan, and Mexico, formed in 2016. Together, OPEC+ members account for about 40% of global oil production and coordinate output levels to manage prices.

The global weighted average capacity factor of solar PV improved from 14% in 2010 to 18% in 2022, reflecting better panel technology, improved tracking systems that follow the sun, and smarter site selection for maximum irradiance. Single-axis tracking systems can boost output by 20–30% compared to fixed-tilt installations.

The UK became the first major economy to phase out coal from electricity generation entirely, closing its last coal-fired power station in September 2024. This marked the end of coal power in the nation that started the Industrial Revolution with coal over 200 years ago.

source.name: UK Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

text: Cobalt, a critical mineral used in many lithium-ion battery chemistries, is largely mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which holds over 70% of global reserves. Concerns about supply chain ethics and geopolitical concentration have driven research into cobalt-free battery chemistries like lithium iron phosphate (LFP).

Electricity represents only about 20% of final global energy consumption today; the remaining 80% is used directly as heat and as transportation fuel. Fully decarbonizing energy requires not just clean electricity, but electrifying or finding low-carbon alternatives for all those other end uses.

The Gulf Cooperation Council countries — Saudi Arabia, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman — together hold over 40% of the world's proven oil reserves and over 20% of natural gas reserves. Their sovereign wealth funds, built on oil revenues, manage trillions of dollars in global assets.

Induction cooking is about 84% energy-efficient compared to roughly 40% for gas stoves, because it heats the pan directly via electromagnetic fields rather than heating the air around it. Transitioning from gas to induction cooking also eliminates the indoor air pollution associated with gas combustion.

The world's most efficient gas turbine, GE's HA-class combined-cycle plant, achieved a record 64% thermal efficiency in testing. This means 64% of the energy in natural gas is converted to electricity — compared to just 33–40% for older steam plants.

Direct air capture (DAC) technology pulls CO2 directly out of the atmosphere using chemical processes. The world's largest DAC plant, Orca, built in Iceland by Climeworks, can capture just 4,000 tonnes of CO2 per year — a tiny fraction of global annual emissions of over 37 billion tonnes.

Australia has some of the world's best solar, wind, and geothermal resources and is developing plans to become a major exporter of green hydrogen and green ammonia to Asia. The Sun Cable project, if built, would transmit solar power from Australia to Singapore via a 4,200-km undersea cable.

Nuclear power plants produce about 2,500 tonnes of high-level radioactive waste globally each year, which must be isolated from the biosphere for tens of thousands of years. Finland is building the world's first permanent deep geological repository for high-level nuclear waste, known as Onkalo.

Electricity storage duration is a key challenge for renewable integration: while lithium-ion batteries are cost-effective for 2–4 hour storage, the grid also needs 12-hour, 24-hour, and seasonal storage. Gravity-based, compressed air, hydrogen, and thermal storage are all being developed to fill longer-duration storage gaps.

Gravity-based energy storage systems — like Energy Vault's giant concrete blocks lifted by cranes — store energy as gravitational potential energy, then release it as the blocks descend through generators. These systems use cheap, abundant materials and have very long operational lifetimes with minimal degradation.

The world's first electricity-generating windmill was built in 1887 by Scottish inventor James Blyth in Marykirk, Scotland, to power his holiday cottage. Independently, American inventor Charles Brush built a larger 12-kilowatt wind turbine in Cleveland, Ohio, the same year.

The average efficiency of global coal power plants is only about 35–38%, meaning more than 60% of the energy in coal is wasted as heat. Switching older, inefficient coal plants to modern ultra-supercritical designs achieving 45% efficiency would meaningfully reduce CO2 emissions from coal.

IRENA estimates that achieving a 1.5°C pathway requires global renewable energy capacity to reach at least 11,000 gigawatts by 2030 — tripling from 2022 levels. At COP28 in Dubai in 2023, over 130 countries pledged to do exactly this.

The Black Sea's deep waters are rich in hydrogen sulfide gas — a byproduct of anaerobic decomposition in oxygen-depleted layers. Researchers have proposed harnessing this naturally occurring gas as an energy source, though the technology remains experimental.

The levelized cost of energy (LCOE) from rooftop solar for homeowners in many sunny regions has fallen below the retail price of grid electricity, making self-generated solar cheaper than buying from the utility. This 'socket parity' is driving explosive growth in residential solar installations worldwide.

Tidal lagoons — artificial enclosed coastal basins that capture and release tidal water through turbines — could generate predictable, low-carbon electricity. The proposed Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon in Wales would be the world's first purpose-built tidal lagoon power plant if constructed.

Approximately 1 billion people gained access to electricity for the first time between 2010 and 2022, largely through grid expansion and off-grid solar. Despite this remarkable progress, the rate of electrification must further accelerate to meet the UN's universal energy access goal by 2030.

Mini-grids — small electricity networks serving villages or communities with local generation, often solar plus storage — are increasingly seen as the most cost-effective way to bring power to remote populations. The IEA estimates mini-grids will serve around 490 million people by 2030 in a universal access scenario.

The concept of 'prosumers' — energy consumers who also produce electricity, typically through rooftop solar — is fundamentally changing the electricity market. In some countries, prosumers feed significant amounts of electricity back to the grid, challenging traditional utility business models.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) of the United States is the world's largest emergency oil supply, storing up to 714 million barrels of crude oil in underground salt caverns along the Gulf Coast. It was established after the 1973 oil embargo to provide a buffer against supply disruptions.

Saudi Aramco, the Saudi national oil company, is the world's most valuable company by revenue and the single largest emitter of greenhouse gases among corporate entities. Its Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia is the world's largest conventional oil field, producing about 3.8 million barrels per day.

The Atacama Large Array solar project in Chile achieved a record-low auction price of $0.0197 per kilowatt-hour in 2016 — at that time the cheapest electricity ever contracted anywhere in the world. Such low prices were inconceivable just five years earlier and signaled a permanent transformation of energy economics.

The melting of Arctic sea ice is opening new shipping routes — particularly the Northern Sea Route along Russia's Arctic coast — which could reduce shipping distances between Europe and Asia by up to 40%. However, this route requires icebreaker escorts for much of the year and is deeply linked to climate change.

A hydrogen fuel cell vehicle like the Toyota Mirai can travel about 650 kilometers on a full tank of compressed hydrogen, refueling in under five minutes — comparable to conventional vehicles. However, hydrogen refueling infrastructure remains sparse outside Japan, South Korea, and parts of California.

The world's largest floating offshore wind farm is the Hywind Tampen project off Norway, with a capacity of 88 megawatts. Floating wind turbines can be deployed in water depths greater than 60 meters — unlocking vast ocean areas with excellent wind resources that fixed-bottom turbines cannot reach.

The U.S. Clean Air Act of 1970 was one of the world's first major environmental laws to regulate air pollution from power plants and vehicles. It has been credited with preventing millions of premature deaths and saving trillions of dollars in health costs over its history.

In 2023, for the first time, more money was invested globally in clean energy ($1.77 trillion) than in fossil fuels ($1 trillion). This crossover point is widely regarded as a historic turning point in the global energy transition.

The Kalina cycle is an advanced thermodynamic process that improves the efficiency of geothermal power plants by using a mixture of water and ammonia as the working fluid instead of pure water or steam. It can extract more electricity from lower-temperature geothermal resources.

Modern oil refineries are extraordinarily complex facilities that crack, distill, and chemically transform crude oil into hundreds of products including gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, plastics, fertilizers, pharmaceuticals, and synthetic fabrics. Even in a world shifting to EVs, oil's role as a chemical feedstock will keep demand substantial.

The global energy system emits about 37 billion tonnes of CO2 per year from burning fossil fuels — the highest level ever recorded as of 2023. Reaching net zero by 2050 requires reducing these emissions to near zero while removing residual CO2 with natural sinks and carbon capture technology.

Aluminum production is extraordinarily energy-intensive, requiring about 14–15 kilowatt-hours of electricity per kilogram of aluminum produced. For this reason, aluminum smelters are typically located near cheap, abundant power — historically hydropower — and aluminum is sometimes called 'congealed electricity.'

Recycling aluminum requires only about 5% of the energy needed to produce primary aluminum from bauxite ore, making aluminum recycling one of the most energy-efficient industrial processes. This is why recycled aluminum is economically valuable and is collected and recycled at high rates worldwide.

Fusion energy research has often been described as 'always 30 years away,' but the 2022 ignition milestone at NIF and rapid progress by private fusion companies like Commonwealth Fusion Systems and TAE Technologies have led many experts to revise timelines. Several companies now aim for commercial fusion power in the 2030s.

Methane hydrates — ice-like structures in which methane is trapped in a lattice of water molecules — exist in vast quantities on the ocean floor and in Arctic permafrost. Their total carbon content may exceed all other fossil fuels combined, and their potential release due to warming temperatures is a serious climate concern.

The microwave oven was invented accidentally in 1945 when Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had melted while he was testing a radar magnetron. Microwave cooking is significantly more energy-efficient than conventional ovens because it heats food directly rather than the surrounding air.

South Korea's KSTAR (Korean Superconducting Tokamak Advanced Research) reactor maintained a plasma temperature of 100 million degrees Celsius — seven times hotter than the Sun's core — for a record 48 seconds in 2024. Sustaining high-temperature plasma long enough for net energy gain is one of fusion energy's key challenges.

The energy poverty trap — where lack of affordable energy prevents economic development, which in turn prevents investment in energy — is a key reason why energy access is central to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. Studies show that each $1 invested in energy access can unlock $15 or more in economic activity in low-income communities.

The Rance Tidal Power Plant in France, operating since 1966, generates electricity during both incoming (flood) and outgoing (ebb) tides by running its turbines in both directions, effectively doubling its generation opportunities. This bidirectional generation is a key advantage of tidal barrage technology.

The concept of the 'energy internet' envisions a future grid where millions of distributed energy sources — solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, EVs — are connected and managed by intelligent software in real time. Like the information internet, such a decentralized energy web could be more resilient, democratic, and efficient than today's centralized grids.

Renewables are now the default choice for new electricity generation in most of the world — not for environmental reasons alone but because they are simply the cheapest option. The IEA's 2023 World Energy Outlook concluded that the era of fossil fuel growth is over, with demand for oil, gas, and coal all expected to peak before 2030.

Pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) is the world's largest form of grid-scale energy storage, accounting for over 90% of global storage capacity at roughly 170 GW installed. Water is pumped uphill to a reservoir during low-demand periods and released through turbines when demand is high.

Compressed Air Energy Storage (CAES) works by using surplus electricity to compress air into underground caverns or tanks, then releasing it through a turbine to generate power on demand. The world's first commercial CAES plant opened in Huntorf, Germany in 1978 and still operates today.

Flywheel energy storage systems store kinetic energy in a rapidly spinning rotor and can respond to grid fluctuations in milliseconds — far faster than chemical batteries. Beacon Power's 20 MW flywheel plant in Stephentown, New York was one of the first commercial flywheel facilities used for frequency regulation.

Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolyte solutions held in external tanks, meaning capacity can be scaled independently of power by simply enlarging the tanks. Vanadium redox flow batteries are the most commercially mature type and can last 20+ years with minimal degradation.

Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte of conventional lithium-ion cells with a solid material, offering higher energy density, faster charging, and improved safety. Toyota announced plans to commercialize solid-state batteries for electric vehicles by 2027–2028, targeting a 1,200 km range per charge.

ITER (International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor) is the world's largest fusion experiment, under construction in Cadarache, France, with 35 nations collaborating. When complete, ITER aims to produce 500 MW of fusion power from just 50 MW of input heating — a Q factor of 10.

The National Ignition Facility (NIF) at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory achieved fusion ignition on December 5, 2022 — the first time a fusion reaction produced more energy than the laser energy delivered to the target. The experiment yielded 3.15 megajoules from 2.05 megajoules of laser input.

A tokamak is a donut-shaped magnetic confinement device that uses powerful magnetic fields to confine plasma at temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius — hotter than the Sun's core. The design was pioneered by Soviet physicists Igor Tamm and Andrei Sakharov in the 1950s.

A stellarator, unlike a tokamak, uses a twisted magnetic field created entirely by external coils — eliminating the need for plasma current and making it more stable for continuous operation. The Wendelstein 7-X in Greifswald, Germany is the world's most advanced stellarator.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics

text: Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) are nuclear fission reactors with a capacity of 300 MW or less, designed to be factory-built and then shipped to site, reducing construction costs and time compared to conventional large reactors. More than 80 SMR designs are under development worldwide.

NuScale Power's VOYGR SMR design became the first small modular reactor design to receive approval from the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission in 2022. Each NuScale module generates 77 MW of electricity and can be combined in arrays of up to 12 units.

Thorium is three to four times more abundant in Earth's crust than uranium and produces far less long-lived radioactive waste when used as nuclear fuel. India, which holds about a quarter of the world's thorium reserves, is developing a three-stage nuclear program to eventually run on thorium.

Liquid fluoride thorium reactors (LFTRs) use molten salt as both fuel and coolant, operating at atmospheric pressure rather than the high pressures of conventional water-cooled reactors, potentially making them safer and cheaper to build. Oak Ridge National Laboratory ran a molten salt reactor experiment successfully from 1965 to 1969.

Green hydrogen is produced by using renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen through electrolysis, releasing zero carbon dioxide. It is considered crucial for decarbonizing heavy industry, shipping, and aviation where direct electrification is difficult.

Blue hydrogen is produced from natural gas via steam methane reforming, with the resulting carbon dioxide captured and stored underground (CCS). Critics argue the process still leaks methane and the CCS infrastructure is expensive, making blue hydrogen's climate benefit contested.

Grey hydrogen — the most common form today — is produced from natural gas without capturing the CO₂ byproduct, making it the most carbon-intensive hydrogen type. About 95% of hydrogen produced globally in 2023 was grey or blue, with green hydrogen still representing a tiny fraction.

Smart grids use digital communication technology, sensors, and advanced analytics to manage electricity flow in real time, optimizing supply and demand across the network. The U.S. smart grid investment in the 2009 Recovery Act totaled $4.5 billion and laid the foundation for modern grid modernization programs.

Microgrids are localized electricity grids that can operate independently ('island') from the main grid during outages, providing resilience for hospitals, military bases, universities, and remote communities. California alone had over 400 operational microgrids by 2023.

Energy poverty — the lack of access to reliable, affordable modern energy services — affects roughly 730 million people who still lack electricity access globally as of 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for about three-quarters of that population.

Africa holds about 60% of the world's best solar resources yet generates only about 3% of global solar power. The African Development Bank's Desert to Power initiative aims to install 10 GW of solar capacity in the Sahel region by 2030, providing electricity to 250 million people.

Off-grid solar and mini-grid solutions have connected more than 420 million people to electricity in developing nations since 2010, often bypassing the need for expensive centralized grid infrastructure. Pay-as-you-go solar models pioneered in East Africa have been replicated across 40+ countries.

Offshore wind turbines can be placed in the sea where winds are stronger and more consistent than on land, and the turbines can be built larger because there are no transportation constraints. The Hornsea 2 wind farm off the UK coast, completed in 2022, was the world's largest offshore wind farm at 1.3 GW.

Floating offshore wind technology allows turbines to be anchored in waters deeper than 60 meters where fixed-bottom foundations are not practical, opening up vast ocean areas with excellent wind resources. Norway's Hywind Tampen, operational since 2022, is the world's largest floating wind farm.

Floating solar photovoltaic (FPV) installations are placed on water bodies such as reservoirs, lakes, and flooded quarries, conserving land and reducing water evaporation by up to 80%. Global floating solar capacity surpassed 4 GW by 2023, with China, South Korea, and India leading deployments.

Perovskite solar cells have demonstrated rapid efficiency gains, climbing from about 3.8% in 2009 to over 26% in 2023 in laboratory settings — matching or exceeding commercial silicon cells. Their low-cost materials and simple manufacturing processes make them a leading candidate for next-generation solar technology.

Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) plants use mirrors or lenses to focus sunlight onto a receiver, generating heat that drives a steam turbine. Unlike standard photovoltaics, CSP can store heat in molten salt for hours, allowing electricity generation after sunset.

The Noor Ouarzazate solar complex in Morocco is one of the world's largest CSP plants, with a total capacity of 580 MW. It stores enough thermal energy in molten salt to supply electricity for up to three hours after the sun sets.

Wave energy converters capture the kinetic and potential energy of ocean surface waves to generate electricity, with the global resource estimated at more than 2 TW — comparable to current global electricity consumption. Despite decades of R&D, wave energy has yet to achieve commercial scale due to the harsh ocean environment.

Tidal stream generators are submerged turbines that extract energy from tidal currents in the same way wind turbines extract energy from wind, with the advantage that tidal flows are highly predictable. MeyGen in Scotland's Pentland Firth is the world's largest tidal stream array, with 6 MW installed by 2023.

Biogas is produced by the anaerobic digestion of organic waste — food scraps, animal manure, sewage sludge, and agricultural residues — and is primarily composed of methane and CO₂. It can be used directly for heating and cooking, or upgraded to biomethane and injected into natural gas networks.

Biomass energy — burning organic materials such as wood pellets, agricultural residues, and dedicated energy crops — supplies about 10% of global primary energy, making it the largest single renewable energy source by volume. However, its sustainability depends heavily on how the biomass is grown and harvested.

Energy efficiency standards for appliances — such as refrigerators, air conditioners, and lighting — have been among the most cost-effective climate and energy policies worldwide. The U.S. appliance standards program has since 1987 saved consumers more than $2 trillion in energy bills.

Building energy codes set minimum efficiency requirements for new construction and major renovations, covering insulation, windows, HVAC systems, and lighting. Buildings account for about 40% of global final energy consumption, making codes a critical lever for reducing long-term energy demand.

District heating systems distribute heat generated at a central plant through a network of insulated pipes to residential and commercial buildings, and are far more efficient than individual boilers. Denmark heats about 64% of its buildings via district heating, with a growing share powered by geothermal and waste heat.

Heat pumps move heat from one place to another using electricity — from the outside air, ground, or water into a building — delivering 2 to 5 units of heat energy for every unit of electrical energy consumed. They are one of the most efficient heating technologies available and can also provide cooling in reverse.

Sales of heat pumps surpassed gas boilers in Europe for the first time in 2022, with over 3 million units sold. Norway leads heat pump adoption with 60% of all homes equipped with one, partly driven by its cheap hydroelectric electricity.

The first practical steam engine, developed by Thomas Newcomen in 1712, was used to pump water out of coal mines in England. James Watt's improved version in 1769 — adding a separate condenser — dramatically increased efficiency and unlocked the Industrial Revolution.

Thomas Edison opened the world's first central power station, Pearl Street Station in Manhattan, on September 4, 1882, supplying direct current electricity to 85 customers. Within 14 months, the station was powering more than 500 buildings with 10,000 lamps.

The 'War of Currents' in the late 1880s pitted Thomas Edison's direct current (DC) system against Nikola Tesla and George Westinghouse's alternating current (AC) system. AC ultimately won because it could be transmitted over much greater distances at high voltages and then stepped down for consumer use.

The world's first nuclear power plant to generate electricity for a commercial grid was Obninsk, in the Soviet Union, which began operation on June 27, 1954. It had a capacity of just 5 MW but demonstrated the viability of civilian nuclear power.

The first commercial-scale solar farm in the United States was the 1 MW Lugo solar project in Hesperia, California, built in 1982. Solar PV costs have since fallen by more than 99% — from roughly $76/watt in 1977 to under $0.20/watt by 2023.

The oil embargo by Arab members of OPEC in October 1973 triggered the first global oil crisis, quadrupling oil prices in just months and exposing the vulnerability of Western economies to energy supply disruptions. The crisis accelerated investments in nuclear power, coal, and early renewable energy research.

Denmark pivoted from near-total dependence on imported oil to a diversified, renewable-heavy energy system following the 1973 oil crisis, later becoming a global leader in wind power. By 2023, wind supplied over 50% of Denmark's annual electricity consumption.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 2022 Mitigation report found that solar and wind electricity now cost less than fossil fuel alternatives in most of the world, identifying rapid renewable scaling as the single largest mitigation opportunity this decade.

Gravity-based energy storage systems use excess electricity to lift heavy masses — such as weights in mine shafts or concrete blocks — and recover energy by lowering them through generators. Gravitricity's prototype in Edinburgh and Energy Vault's block-stacking crane systems are among the projects pioneering this approach.

The levelized cost of energy (LCOE) is a standard metric comparing the lifetime costs of different electricity generation technologies per kilowatt-hour. By 2023, utility-scale solar PV had an average global LCOE of $0.049/kWh — cheaper than any fossil fuel source and down 90% since 2010.

The Pacific Intertie is a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission line running 1,361 km from the Columbia River in Oregon to the Los Angeles area, transmitting up to 3,100 MW of hydroelectric power. HVDC is more efficient than AC over very long distances and is key to connecting remote renewable resources.

Virtual Power Plants (VPPs) aggregate thousands of distributed energy resources — rooftop solar, home batteries, smart appliances, and EV chargers — and control them remotely to behave like a single large power plant. Australia's largest VPP, operated by AGL, has linked over 1,000 home battery systems.

Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) technology allows electric vehicles to feed stored electricity back into the power grid during peak demand, turning millions of car batteries into a distributed storage resource. Japan leads V2G adoption after the 2011 earthquake showed the value of using EV batteries as backup power.

The Beaufort Scale was developed by British naval officer Sir Francis Beaufort in 1805 to categorize wind speed, but today the wind industry relies on the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) turbine classes — Class I for high-wind sites, Class III for low-wind sites — to match turbine design to location.

China installed more solar and wind capacity in 2023 alone than the entire rest of the world combined, adding approximately 300 GW of renewables in a single year. China is now the world's largest producer and consumer of renewable electricity.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) involves capturing CO₂ from industrial processes or power plants and injecting it into deep geological formations for permanent storage. The Sleipner CCS project in the North Sea, operated by Equinor since 1996, was the world's first commercial-scale CCS facility.

Hydropower remains the world's largest source of renewable electricity, generating about 4,200 TWh per year — roughly 15% of global electricity production. The Three Gorges Dam in China, the world's largest power station by installed capacity, generates about 100 TWh annually.

Nuclear power currently supplies about 10% of the world's electricity from 413 operating reactors in 32 countries. France relies on nuclear for about 70% of its electricity — the highest share of any nation — and exports significant amounts to its neighbors.

The Capacity Factor of an energy source measures how much energy it actually produces compared to its maximum possible output. Offshore wind has a capacity factor of around 40–50%, compared to ~25% for onshore wind and ~15–22% for solar PV, making offshore wind especially productive per unit of installed capacity.

The Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) signed by President Biden in August 2022 is the largest climate and clean energy investment in U.S. history, providing roughly $369 billion in energy security and climate provisions. Analysts project it will drive 1 trillion dollars in clean energy investment by 2032.

Power-to-X technologies use surplus renewable electricity to produce fuels or chemicals — such as green hydrogen, ammonia, methanol, or synthetic jet fuel — storing renewable energy in chemical form for sectors that are hard to electrify. Ammonia produced from green hydrogen is being explored as a zero-carbon shipping fuel.

Demand response programs pay electricity customers — factories, commercial buildings, and even households — to reduce or shift consumption during periods of peak demand or grid stress. California's demand response programs have successfully reduced peak demand by over 2,000 MW, equivalent to several power plants.

Agrivoltaics — the co-location of solar panels and agricultural crops on the same land — can simultaneously produce food and electricity, boosting land productivity by up to 70%. Shade from panels can reduce crop water requirements and protect fragile crops like berries from hail and excessive heat.

source.name: Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems

text: The global energy transition requires an unprecedented scale of critical minerals — lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, and rare earths — for batteries, wind turbines, and solar panels. The IEA estimates that a Net Zero pathway requires six times more mineral inputs by 2040 than today.

Sodium-ion batteries are emerging as a lower-cost alternative to lithium-ion batteries for stationary grid storage because sodium is far more abundant and less expensive than lithium. CATL, the world's largest battery manufacturer, launched commercial sodium-ion battery production in 2023.

The concept of 'energy returned on energy invested' (EROI) measures how much usable energy is produced for every unit of energy spent in harvesting it. Modern wind turbines have an EROI of around 20:1, solar PV around 10:1, and oil extraction has dropped from roughly 100:1 in the early 20th century to under 20:1 today.

Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) involve creating or enhancing permeability in hot dry rock by injecting water at high pressure, potentially unlocking geothermal energy in regions without natural hydrothermal resources. Fervo Energy successfully demonstrated a commercial EGS project in Nevada in 2023, a milestone for this technology.

Liquid air energy storage (LAES) cools air to −196 °C to liquefy it, stores the liquid in insulated tanks, then re-gasifies it to drive a turbine when power is needed. Highview Power's CRYOBattery in Manchester, UK, is the world's first commercial LAES facility, with a capacity of 50 MW / 250 MWh.

The Swanson's Law describes the observed trend of solar PV module prices falling roughly 20% for every doubling of cumulative shipped volume, similar to Moore's Law for semiconductors. This learning-rate effect has made solar the fastest cost-declining energy technology in history.

The Betz limit, derived by German physicist Albert Betz in 1919, states that a wind turbine can extract at most 59.3% of the kinetic energy in the wind. Modern large turbines achieve aerodynamic efficiencies of around 45–50%, very close to this theoretical maximum.

The global electricity system lost approximately 8% of all electricity generated in transmission and distribution in 2022 — roughly equal to the total electricity generation of all of Sub-Saharan Africa. Reducing these losses through better infrastructure and smart grid technology is a major efficiency opportunity.

The Sahara Desert alone theoretically receives enough solar energy each day to power the entire world 7,000 times over. The DESERTEC concept proposed transmitting solar and wind energy from North Africa and the Middle East to Europe via HVDC cables, though geopolitical and cost challenges have slowed its development.

Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) exploits the temperature difference between warm surface seawater and cold deep-ocean water to run a heat engine and generate electricity. The resource is most viable in tropical regions and could theoretically supply several terawatts, but high capital costs have prevented large-scale deployment.

Piezoelectric materials generate electrical charge when mechanically stressed, and researchers are exploring harvesting ambient vibrations — from footsteps on pedestrian tiles, traffic on roads, and machinery — to power sensors and low-energy devices. Tokyo's Shibuya station tested piezoelectric floor tiles to capture energy from pedestrian traffic as early as 2008.

The Paris Agreement of 2015, signed by 196 parties, commits nations to limiting global warming to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C. Achieving the 1.5°C goal requires cutting global CO₂ emissions by approximately 45% by 2030 and reaching net zero by around 2050.

Electrolyzers used to produce green hydrogen come in three main types: alkaline (the most mature), proton exchange membrane (PEM, faster response), and solid oxide (the most efficient). PEM electrolyzers, developed originally for space applications, pair especially well with variable renewable energy sources.

Rooftop solar has become the fastest-growing electricity source in Australia, where over 3.6 million homes — roughly one in three — had solar panels by 2023. This has led to midday grid prices frequently going negative in some Australian states, as solar generation overwhelms demand.

The Ivanpah Solar Electric Generating System in California's Mojave Desert uses 173,500 heliostat mirrors to focus sunlight onto boilers atop three 140-metre towers, generating 377 MW of electricity. It is one of the largest operational CSP tower plants in the world.

Distributed energy resources (DERs) — small-scale generators, batteries, EVs, and smart appliances located at or near the point of use — are transforming grid management from a top-down hierarchical system to a two-way, decentralized network. The IEA projects that DERs could supply 25% of global electricity by 2040.
