The Itaipu Dam on the border of Brazil and Paraguay was the world's largest hydroelectric facility by installed capacity for 25 years (1984–2009) and still supplies about 15% of Brazil's electricity and 88% of Paraguay's. It generates roughly 100 TWh per year.

Energy intensity — the amount of energy used per unit of GDP — has been declining globally for decades, meaning the world is getting more economically productive from each unit of energy. However, absolute energy consumption has still risen because GDP growth has outpaced efficiency gains.

The Tokamak Energy company and Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) are private companies developing compact high-temperature superconducting tokamaks, aiming to achieve commercial fusion power far sooner than ITER. CFS's SPARC device, targeting a Q>2 experiment around 2025, uses high-field magnets made from newly available REBCO superconducting tape.

The Global Wind Atlas, developed by the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) for the World Bank, provides free, high-resolution wind resource data for every location on Earth, enabling nations to identify optimal wind farm sites. It has been used to plan projects in over 100 countries.

Geothermal heat pumps — also called ground-source heat pumps — exploit the relatively constant ground temperature of around 10–15°C at shallow depths to provide highly efficient heating in winter and cooling in summer. A single geothermal heat pump installation can reduce home heating energy use by 25–70% compared to conventional systems.

The concept of 'negawatts' — coined by energy analyst Amory Lovins in 1983 — describes electricity saved through conservation and efficiency as equivalent in value to electricity generated. Lovins and the Rocky Mountain Institute have argued that the cheapest power plant is one that never needs to be built.

The Allam-Fetvedt Cycle is a novel natural gas power generation technology that burns fuel in pure oxygen and supercritical CO₂, producing a stream of near-pure CO₂ that can be easily captured and sequestered. NET Power's first commercial-scale plant in Texas began testing in 2021.

Long-duration energy storage (LDES) — systems that can store electricity for 8 to 100+ hours — is considered essential for deeply decarbonized power grids that rely heavily on variable wind and solar. Technologies including iron-air batteries, hydrogen storage, and thermal storage are competing to fill this gap.

Form Energy's iron-air battery stores energy for up to 100 hours at very low cost by rusting iron pellets during discharge (iron + oxygen → rust, releasing electrons) and reversing the process during charging. The technology is based on Earth-abundant materials and targets a cost 10 times lower than lithium-ion for long-duration storage.

The Shockley-Queisser limit sets the maximum theoretical efficiency of a single-junction solar cell at approximately 33.7% under standard illumination, due to thermodynamic losses from photons above and below the bandgap. Multi-junction concentrator solar cells using three or more layers have exceeded 47% efficiency in laboratory conditions.

Energy communities are groups of citizens, businesses, and local authorities that jointly own and manage renewable energy assets — typically wind farms or solar installations — sharing the economic benefits locally. Over 9,000 community energy projects operate across Europe, generating power for millions of households.

Wind power curtailment — shutting down turbines despite available wind because the grid cannot absorb all the electricity — is a growing challenge in countries with high renewable penetration. In 2022, China curtailed an estimated 15 TWh of wind power, equivalent to the annual electricity use of millions of homes.

The European Union's REPowerEU plan, launched in response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, aims to end EU dependence on Russian fossil fuels by 2027 and accelerate the renewable energy transition. It raised the EU's 2030 renewable energy target from 40% to 45% of final energy consumption.

The Integrated Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) converts coal or biomass into a synthetic gas ('syngas'), which is then cleaned and burned in a gas turbine, achieving higher efficiency and lower emissions than conventional coal plants. IGCC plants can also be adapted for pre-combustion carbon capture.

Pakistan's Thar Coal Field in Sindh province is one of the world's largest lignite deposits, estimated at 175 billion tonnes, yet remains largely undeveloped. Its potential development raises major carbon emission concerns at a time when international financing for new coal projects has all but dried up.

Nuclear fusion produces about four million times more energy per kilogram of fuel than coal and about four times more than fission, with hydrogen isotopes as fuel. A single kilogram of fusion fuel (deuterium + tritium) could in principle generate as much energy as roughly 10 million kg of coal.

The Breakthrough Energy Ventures fund, co-founded by Bill Gates and other major investors in 2016, has committed over $2 billion to early-stage clean energy startups including companies working on next-generation geothermal, fusion, long-duration storage, and green hydrogen.

Offshore wind turbine blades can exceed 100 metres in length, making each turbine tip-to-tip span greater than the wingspan of an Airbus A380. Siemens Gamesa's SG 14-236 DD offshore turbine has a rotor diameter of 236 metres and a rated capacity of 15 MW per unit.

Iceland is the only country in the world to meet over 99% of its electricity demand from renewable sources — primarily geothermal and hydropower — year-round. Its energy abundance supports an energy-intensive aluminum smelting industry that exports metal produced at some of the world's lowest carbon intensities.

Solar irradiance — the power per unit area received from the Sun — averages about 1,361 W/m² at the top of Earth's atmosphere, known as the solar constant. By the time sunlight reaches Earth's surface, about half is lost to atmospheric scattering and absorption.

The World Bank's Scaling Solar program provides bundled services to help African and other developing-country governments procure utility-scale solar at competitive prices, having facilitated projects in Zambia, Senegal, Madagascar, and other nations. Zambia's first Scaling Solar auction in 2017 produced electricity at 6 US cents/kWh — the cheapest in Africa at the time.

Interconnected electricity grids allow countries to trade power across borders, improving reliability and enabling higher renewable penetration by smoothing out local surpluses and deficits. The European electricity market spans 36 countries and trades hundreds of terawatt-hours per year.

The specific energy density of aviation jet fuel (approximately 43 MJ/kg) remains far higher than even the best lithium-ion batteries (~0.9 MJ/kg), which is why fully electric long-haul aviation is still impractical and why sustainable aviation fuels (SAFs) are attracting billions in investment.

The global average electricity access rate reached 91% in 2021, up from 84% in 2010, driven by major gains in South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh alone connected over 100 million people to electricity in a decade, including through the world's largest off-grid solar home system program.

The Masdar City project in Abu Dhabi, UAE, was conceived in 2008 as the world's first planned zero-carbon, zero-waste city, powered entirely by renewable energy. While the most ambitious aspects of the project were scaled back, Masdar City has become a major hub for clean energy research and hosts the headquarters of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA).

Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries have a theoretical energy density five times higher than lithium-ion, using cheap, abundant sulfur as the cathode material. Researchers at Monash University demonstrated a Li-S cell in 2020 with a record specific energy of 543 Wh/kg.

The sun's core temperature reaches about 15 million degrees Celsius, producing energy through nuclear fusion where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium. The energy generated in the Sun's core takes approximately 100,000 years to reach the surface and only 8 minutes to travel to Earth.

Direct air capture (DAC) technology removes CO₂ directly from the atmosphere using large fans and chemical sorbents, addressing emissions that are too dispersed to capture at source. Climeworks' Orca plant in Iceland, the world's first commercial DAC facility, opened in 2021 and can capture 4,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year.

The global electricity storage market installed a record 45 GW / 100 GWh of battery storage in 2023, more than doubling 2022 figures, driven by falling lithium-ion prices and grid-scale project procurement. The IEA projects 1,500 GW of storage is needed by 2030 to meet climate targets.

Inertia in the power grid — the physical flywheel effect of spinning generators that resists sudden frequency changes — is provided naturally by coal and nuclear plants but must be emulated by new 'synthetic inertia' software in inverter-based renewable systems. Australia's South Australia grid has pioneered synthetic inertia services as it approaches 100% renewable electricity.

Black silicon solar cells use a nanoscale textured surface that traps light more effectively than conventional silicon, achieving very low reflectance. Aalto University and Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya researchers demonstrated black silicon cells with efficiencies exceeding 22%, competitive with standard commercial cells.

The average coal power plant globally has an efficiency of about 37%, meaning 63% of the thermal energy in coal is wasted as heat. Ultra-supercritical coal plants operating at higher steam temperatures and pressures can reach 45–50% efficiency.

The global shipping industry emits about 2.9% of global greenhouse gases and faces intense pressure to decarbonize. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) adopted a revised 2023 strategy targeting net-zero shipping emissions by 2050.

Waste-to-energy (WtE) plants burn non-recyclable waste to generate electricity and heat, recovering energy from materials that would otherwise go to landfill. Sweden operates 34 WtE plants and imports waste from other European countries to run them, converting over 6 million tonnes of waste to energy annually.

India is the world's third-largest electricity producer and consumer, and added over 18 GW of renewable energy capacity in 2023 alone. India's National Green Hydrogen Mission, launched in 2023, targets 5 million tonnes per year of green hydrogen production by 2030.

The duck curve is a phenomenon observed in power grid management where solar generation in the middle of the day reduces net demand, creating a sharp ramp-up requirement in the evening when solar fades and demand remains high — the curve resembles a duck's back. California's grid regularly experiences this pattern.

Redox flow batteries using zinc-bromine chemistry offer low cost per kWh for multi-hour storage and have a longer cycle life than most lithium-ion systems. Eos Energy Enterprises commercializes zinc-hybrid flow batteries for behind-the-meter and grid-scale storage applications.

Nuclear power's carbon footprint — measured over its full lifecycle including construction and fuel processing — is among the lowest of any electricity source at around 12 gCO₂eq/kWh, comparable to wind and lower than solar. The IPCC identifies nuclear as a low-carbon technology essential for climate mitigation.

The United States produces more oil than any other country in history, pumping over 13 million barrels per day in 2023 — surpassing the previous global record set by Saudi Arabia. The shale revolution, enabled by hydraulic fracturing (fracking) and horizontal drilling, drove this dramatic rise.

The global electricity grid is the largest machine ever built by humanity, with interconnected networks of generators, transformers, transmission lines, and distribution systems spanning entire continents. The North American grid alone has over 450,000 miles of high-voltage transmission lines.

Superconducting magnetic energy storage (SMES) systems store energy in the magnetic field of a superconducting coil cooled to near absolute zero. SMES devices can release large amounts of energy in fractions of a second, making them ideal for power quality applications and grid stabilization.

The first wind turbine to generate electricity was built by Charles F. Brush in Cleveland, Ohio in 1888. It had a 17-meter diameter rotor with 144 blades and powered 350 incandescent lights via a battery bank — but was quickly superseded by cheaper coal-fired electricity.

The International Solar Energy Society (ISES), founded in 1954 in the United States, is the oldest renewable energy organization in the world. Its formation came just two years after Bell Labs demonstrated the first practical silicon solar cell in 1954.

The world's first offshore wind farm was Vindeby, installed off the coast of Denmark in 1991 with 11 turbines of 450 kW each — a total of 4.95 MW. Vindeby was decommissioned in 2017 after 26 years of operation and became the first offshore wind farm to be dismantled.

Bell Labs' invention of the silicon solar cell in April 1954 by Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller, and Gerald Pearson achieved an efficiency of approximately 6%, compared to the less than 1% of prior selenium-based cells. The New York Times called it 'the beginning of a new era, leading eventually to the realization of one of mankind's most cherished dreams — the harnessing of the almost limitless energy of the sun.'

Power sector carbon intensity — CO₂ emitted per kWh of electricity generated — fell in the OECD countries from 410 gCO₂/kWh in 2000 to 230 gCO₂/kWh by 2022, a 44% reduction driven by fuel switching from coal to gas and renewables. The global average in 2022 was around 460 gCO₂/kWh.

Diurnal temperature variation — the daily swing between daytime heat and nighttime cool — in desert regions has been proposed as a basis for thermoelectric power generation. Though the concept remains experimental at scale, thermoelectric generators are already used to power deep-space probes via radioactive decay heat.

Biomass torrefaction — a mild thermal treatment at 200–300°C — converts raw wood chips into a stable, energy-dense pellet similar to coal that can be co-fired in existing coal power plants without major modifications. Torrefied biomass has about 30% higher energy density than regular wood pellets.

HVDC (High Voltage Direct Current) transmission has become preferred for long-distance and undersea cables because it loses less energy over distance than AC and avoids the reactive power problems of long AC lines. The NordLink cable connecting Norway and Germany, at 623 km, is one of the world's longest HVDC undersea cables.

ERCOT, the electricity grid operator for most of Texas, operates largely independently from the rest of the U.S. grid, giving it minimal ability to import emergency power from neighboring states. During the February 2021 winter storm, this isolation contributed to failures that left over 4 million Texans without power for days.

The levelized cost of new onshore wind in the United States fell from roughly $135/MWh in 2010 to around $26/MWh by 2023 — a 81% decline — making it one of the cheapest sources of electricity in American history. This cost reduction was driven by larger turbines, better siting, and competition among manufacturers.

Demand-side flexibility — adjusting when consumers use energy to match renewable generation — is estimated by the IEA to provide up to 500 GW of virtual capacity globally by 2030. Smart thermostats, EV charging timers, and industrial load-shifting are key tools for unlocking this resource.

Passive house (Passivhaus) is a rigorous building energy standard developed in Germany in the early 1990s that achieves energy savings of 75–90% versus conventional construction through super-insulation, triple-glazed windows, and mechanical ventilation with heat recovery. There are now over 65,000 certified Passivhaus buildings worldwide.

The concept of an 'energy island' — an artificial island in the North Sea serving as a hub for offshore wind farms and interconnectors linking multiple countries — was pioneered by Denmark, which began construction of Bornholm Energy Island in 2022. It will eventually connect 10 GW of offshore wind capacity and link Denmark, Germany, and the Netherlands.

Salinity gradient energy — also called osmotic power or blue energy — harvests the potential energy released when fresh river water mixes with salty seawater at estuaries, using pressure-retarded osmosis or reverse electrodialysis membranes. Norway's Statkraft built the world's first osmotic power prototype plant in 2009.

The IEA's 'Net Zero by 2050' roadmap, published in 2021, was the first comprehensive scenario by a major international body showing a pathway to net-zero CO₂ emissions by 2050. Key milestones include no new oil and gas fields approved for development after 2021 and no new unabated coal power plants beyond those already committed.

Microhydro power systems use small turbines installed in streams and rivers to generate electricity at the community or household level, typically producing between 5 kW and 100 kW. In Nepal, over 3,000 micro-hydro plants power more than a million rural households that are beyond the reach of the national grid.

Bifacial solar panels generate electricity from both their front and rear surfaces by capturing reflected light (albedo) from the ground below. They can produce 5–30% more electricity than equivalent monofacial panels depending on ground reflectivity, and have become the dominant product in utility-scale projects.

Green ammonia — produced from green hydrogen and nitrogen via the Haber-Bosch process — is considered one of the most promising zero-carbon fuels for shipping and agriculture, as ammonia can be stored as a liquid at moderate pressure. Global green ammonia capacity is projected to reach 30 million tonnes by 2030.

Concentrated Photovoltaics (CPV) use lenses or mirrors to concentrate sunlight hundreds of times onto small, ultra-high-efficiency multi-junction solar cells. CPV systems can achieve efficiencies exceeding 40%, but require precise solar tracking and work best in high-irradiance, low-cloud locations.

Germany's Energiewende ('energy transition') policy, launched in 2010, aimed to phase out nuclear power and fossil fuels while expanding renewables. By 2023, renewables generated 59% of Germany's electricity, but the country also controversially extended some coal plants after shutting down its last three nuclear reactors in April 2023.

About 2.3 billion people still rely on polluting cooking fuels — solid biomass such as wood, charcoal, dung, and crop waste — causing around 3.2 million premature deaths annually from household air pollution. The IEA's 2030 universal clean cooking target requires 2.5 billion people to gain access to clean cooking solutions.

Fuel cells generate electricity through an electrochemical reaction between hydrogen and oxygen, producing only water as a byproduct — making them a zero-emission power source when fueled by green hydrogen. NASA has used hydrogen fuel cells to power spacecraft since the Gemini missions in the 1960s.

The principle of energy conservation — that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted from one form to another — was formalized by Julius Robert von Mayer, James Prescott Joule, and Hermann von Helmholtz independently in the 1840s. It is now known as the First Law of Thermodynamics.

The Second Law of Thermodynamics states that every energy conversion increases the total entropy of the universe — meaning some energy always becomes unavailable as useful work. This principle explains why no heat engine can ever be 100% efficient and underpins the design of all real-world power systems.

Solar energy accounts for less than 5% of global electricity generation today yet analysts at BloombergNEF project it will become the single largest source of electricity by the early 2030s, surpassing coal, gas, and every other technology. This shift would represent the fastest energy transition in history.

Tidal barrages, like the La Rance facility in Brittany, France — operational since 1966 — capture tidal energy by damming a tidal estuary and passing tidal flow through turbines. La Rance's 240 MW output made it the world's largest tidal power station for over four decades.

Kite-based airborne wind energy systems capture the stronger, more consistent winds available at altitudes of 200–800 m by flying tethered kites or rigid wings that drive generators, either aloft or at the ground station. Makani Power, acquired by Google's parent Alphabet, demonstrated a 600 kW airborne turbine before the project was discontinued in 2020.

The Democratic Republic of Congo's Inga hydropower site on the Congo River has a theoretical potential of 100 GW — more than all of Africa's current installed electricity capacity — if fully developed. Grand Inga, if built, would be the world's largest power station, though financing and governance challenges have stalled the project for decades.

A combined heat and power (CHP) or cogeneration system simultaneously generates electricity and recovers useful heat from the same fuel, achieving overall efficiencies of 70–90% versus 33–45% for conventional electricity-only plants. Hospital, university, and industrial CHP systems are common in Northern Europe.

Costa Rica has generated over 98% of its electricity from renewable sources — primarily hydropower, geothermal, and wind — for several consecutive years. The country ran on 100% renewable electricity for extended periods in 2015, 2016, and again in 2022.

The 'Energy Trilemma' — balancing energy security, energy equity, and environmental sustainability — is a core framework used by the World Energy Council to evaluate national energy systems. Achieving all three simultaneously is extremely difficult and requires difficult trade-offs in policy design.

Modular nuclear power is not new — the U.S. Navy has operated over 500 naval reactors in submarines and aircraft carriers since the 1950s, accumulating over 6,200 reactor-years of safe operation. The compact, reliable designs used by the Navy inspired many modern SMR concepts.

Wind energy's rapid cost decline stems partly from Moore's-Law-like learning effects but also from sheer size growth: the average onshore turbine sold in the U.S. in 2023 had a capacity of 3.1 MW and a hub height of 98 m, up from 1.6 MW and 80 m a decade earlier. Larger turbines capture more wind and produce more electricity per unit of material.

The first practical use of petroleum as an energy fuel began with Edwin Drake's oil well drilled in Titusville, Pennsylvania in 1859. Within a decade, the U.S. had over 5,000 oil wells and petroleum was replacing whale oil for lamps across the country.

The concept of 'peak oil' — the point at which global oil production reaches its maximum rate and begins an irreversible decline — was articulated by geophysicist M. King Hubbert in 1956, who correctly predicted US conventional oil production would peak around 1970. Many analysts now believe we are approaching 'peak oil demand' rather than peak supply.

The global average surface temperature has risen about 1.2°C above pre-industrial levels as of 2023, driven primarily by CO₂ and methane emissions from burning fossil fuels. Every decade since the 1980s has been warmer than the previous one.

Space-based solar power (SBSP) proposes placing large solar arrays in geostationary orbit, where they would collect uninterrupted sunlight 24/7 and beam the energy to Earth as microwaves or laser light. The European Space Agency launched a formal SBSP program in 2022, and the UK National Space Agency has commissioned feasibility studies.

The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), established after the 1973 oil embargo, stores emergency crude oil in underground salt caverns along the Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast. With a capacity of about 714 million barrels, it is the world's largest emergency crude oil stockpile.

Methane (CH₄) is over 80 times more potent than CO₂ as a greenhouse gas over a 20-year period. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane emissions globally, which is why leak detection and methane pledges have become a key focus of climate diplomacy.

Batteries for EVs are typically considered 'end of life' at 70–80% of original capacity but still retain significant value for stationary grid storage. Nissan was an early pioneer of 'second-life' EV battery programs, repurposing used Leaf battery packs to store solar energy at dealerships and homes.

The Carnot efficiency limit defines the maximum theoretical efficiency of any heat engine operating between two temperatures: η = 1 − (T_cold/T_hot), where temperatures are in Kelvin. Modern gas turbines approach 65% efficiency in combined cycle mode — well above earlier steam cycles — by exploiting very high turbine inlet temperatures.

The global subsidy to fossil fuels — including explicit government subsidies and the implicit subsidy of unpriced climate and health externalities — was estimated by the IMF at $5.9 trillion in 2020, equivalent to $11.2 million per minute. Even explicit subsidies alone totaled $7 trillion in 2022.

Morocco's ambition to become Africa's leading renewable energy exporter is backed by a target of 52% renewables in its electricity mix by 2030. The country is developing a green hydrogen export corridor to Europe via undersea pipelines and shipping, leveraging its vast solar and wind resources.

Long-haul hydrogen pipelines repurposed from existing natural gas infrastructure could drastically reduce the cost of delivering green hydrogen across Europe. Germany's existing gas network of 40,000 km is being evaluated for hydrogen compatibility, with about 20% requiring lining or replacement.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway is entirely passive in its cooling — the permafrost keeps the vault cold year-round, using only minimal electricity for lighting and monitoring. Yet rising Arctic temperatures have caused permafrost thaw around the vault, requiring active refrigeration to be installed in 2019.

The 'energy web' or Internet of Energy concept envisions a fully digitized energy system where electricity, data, and value flow bidirectionally among millions of distributed sources and consumers, enabled by AI, blockchain, and IoT sensors. Pilot projects in Brooklyn (NY), Seoul, and Amsterdam have demonstrated peer-to-peer energy trading on local microgrids.

Curtailed electricity from overgeneration — when renewable plants produce more than the grid can absorb — can be 'stored' economically by running energy-intensive industrial processes such as electrolysis, desalination, or aluminum smelting during surplus periods. This concept is known as 'electrofuels' or industrial demand response.

Australia's Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro expansion project will add 2,000 MW of storage capacity and 350,000 MWh of energy storage — enough to power three million homes for a week — by tunneling 27 km through the Snowy Mountains. It is the largest clean energy project in Australia's history.

Concentrating solar thermal power (CSP) plants with molten salt thermal energy storage can provide dispatchable renewable power around the clock. Chile's Cerro Dominador plant, opened in 2021 at 110 MW capacity with 17.5 hours of storage, was Latin America's first commercial CSP plant.

The average American home consumed about 10,500 kWh of electricity in 2022, while the average Indian home consumed around 1,000 kWh — roughly one tenth as much. Closing this gap sustainably while preventing massive carbon emissions is one of the central challenges of global energy equity.

The Trans-Adriatic Pipeline (TAP), which began gas flows in 2020, delivers natural gas from Azerbaijan's Shah Deniz field across Turkey, Greece, Albania, and the Adriatic Sea to Italy — spanning 3,500 km total. It supplied about 10 billion cubic metres of gas to Europe annually, helping diversify away from Russian supplies.

Offshore wind turbines must withstand category-3-equivalent storm loads, including 50-year return-period waves. Monopile foundations — single large steel cylinders driven into the seabed — are the most common foundation type, but jacket structures, tripods, and gravity-based foundations are also used for deeper waters.

The South African township of Soweto has one of the world's highest rates of electricity theft, known locally as 'izinyoka' (snakes), referring to illegal connections. Eskom, South Africa's state utility, estimates it loses over $500 million annually to non-technical losses including theft.

The global data center industry consumed approximately 200–250 TWh of electricity in 2022 — about 1% of global electricity demand — but this is expected to double by 2030 due to AI, cloud computing, and streaming. Making data centers more energy efficient and powering them with renewables is a growing priority.

Bitcoin mining consumed an estimated 127 TWh of electricity globally in 2023 — more than Norway's entire annual electricity consumption. The energy intensity of proof-of-work cryptocurrencies has made them a controversial topic in sustainability discussions.

Geothermal energy is not limited to volcanic regions — shallow ground-source geothermal heat is available nearly everywhere on Earth at depths of 10–100 m, where ground temperature stays relatively constant at the local mean annual air temperature. This makes ground-source heat pumps universally applicable.

Energy literacy — the ability to understand how energy works, how it is converted, and what its costs and impacts are — is considered a critical 21st-century competency. Studies show that households with higher energy literacy make more energy-efficient choices and have lower energy bills.

Chile hosts some of the world's highest solar irradiance in the Atacama Desert, producing up to 3,500 kWh per square metre per year — twice the European average. As a result, Chile regularly achieves negative wholesale electricity prices when solar generation peaks at midday.

The concept of the hydrogen fuel cell vehicle (FCV) was demonstrated by General Motors in 1966 with its Electrovan, which could travel about 200 km on hydrogen. Toyota's Mirai and Honda's Clarity Fuel Cell commercialized the technology beginning in 2015, though FCV sales remain far below battery EVs.

The Sahel region of Africa experiences some of the world's most intense land degradation, but solar energy is enabling a new approach: agrivoltaic 'solar farms' that simultaneously rehabilitate degraded land and produce electricity. The UN's Great Green Wall initiative is exploring integration of solar installations along its 8,000 km reforestation belt.

The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), established in 2009 and headquartered in Abu Dhabi, serves 160+ member countries and publishes authoritative data on renewable energy costs, capacities, and employment. IRENA estimated that the renewable energy sector employed 13.7 million people worldwide in 2022.

Carbon pricing — through carbon taxes or cap-and-trade systems — puts a direct price on CO₂ emissions to incentivize cleaner choices. The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), launched in 2005, is the world's largest carbon market and covers about 40% of EU greenhouse gas emissions.

Nuclear fission releases energy through the splitting of heavy atomic nuclei — typically uranium-235 or plutonium-239 — producing heat used to generate steam and drive turbines. A single uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip contains as much energy as roughly 150 gallons of oil.

Electrolysis of seawater directly — rather than desalinated water — is the subject of intense research because desalination adds cost and energy overhead. A team at MIT developed a direct seawater electrolysis device in 2023 that operates stably for over 100 hours without chlorine-induced degradation.

Solar thermal collectors — flat-plate or evacuated tube devices that heat water or air using sunlight — are distinct from photovoltaics and are among the most widely deployed renewable technologies. China accounts for about 70% of global solar thermal capacity and uses the technology extensively for domestic hot water.

Reactive power management is an essential but invisible aspect of grid operation — alternating current grids require reactive power to maintain voltage levels, and its imbalance can cause voltage collapses. Power factor correction capacitors and new grid-forming inverters are critical tools for managing reactive power in renewable-dominated grids.

The Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), established in 1995, connects the power grids of 12 southern African nations including South Africa, Zimbabwe, Zambia, and Mozambique. It enables regional electricity trading but has been strained by South Africa's severe load-shedding crises of recent years.

Energy recovery ventilation (ERV) systems exchange heat and moisture between incoming fresh air and outgoing stale air in buildings, reducing heating and cooling energy use by 60–80%. They are a key feature of near-zero energy buildings and are mandated by building codes in several Scandinavian countries.

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), fully implemented from 2026, requires importers of steel, cement, aluminum, fertilizer, electricity, and hydrogen to purchase 'carbon certificates' matching the price paid under the EU ETS. It is designed to prevent 'carbon leakage' and level the playing field for EU producers.

The Keeling Curve, initiated by Charles David Keeling at Mauna Loa Observatory in 1958, is the longest continuous record of atmospheric CO₂ concentration. When it began, CO₂ was 315 ppm; by 2023 it exceeded 424 ppm — the highest level in at least 3 million years.

Thorium-powered reactors cannot sustain a chain reaction on their own — thorium-232 must be converted to fissile uranium-233 by absorbing a neutron. This makes thorium reactors inherently proliferation-resistant because the reactor needs an external neutron source and cannot easily be diverted to produce weapons material.

Photovoltaic recycling is becoming an urgent challenge: the first large wave of solar panels installed around 2010–2015 will begin reaching end-of-life (typically 25–30 years) in the mid-2030s. The EU's revised Waste Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) directive was the first regulation globally to mandate PV panel recycling.

Portugal generated more electricity from renewables than it consumed in total for an entire week in October 2016 — a world first for a European country. By 2022 renewables supplied 61% of Portugal's annual electricity, with wind the largest single source.

The International Energy Agency was founded in 1974 in response to the oil crisis, initially as an oil consumers' club to coordinate emergency stockpile releases. It has since evolved into the world's leading energy authority covering all fuels and technologies.

Uranium enrichment — increasing the concentration of the fissile U-235 isotope from its natural 0.7% to 3–5% for reactor fuel — requires vast centrifuge cascades. The same technology can enrich uranium to 90%+ for weapons, creating inherent dual-use proliferation risk that drives international inspections under the Non-Proliferation Treaty.

Electricity storage via underground hydrogen in salt caverns — known as hydrogen storage — can hold vast quantities for seasonal balancing, something impossible with batteries. The UK's HyStock project and Germany's research programs are evaluating retired salt caverns previously used for natural gas as green hydrogen stores.

The Clean Energy Ministerial (CEM), a high-level global forum involving 30+ governments representing 90% of global clean energy investment, has since 2010 coordinated initiatives on offshore wind, electric vehicles, efficient lighting, and clean cooking. It operates through voluntary mission-driven campaigns rather than binding targets.

Solar irradiance varies significantly by latitude, season, and cloud cover, but even cloudy Germany has enough solar resource to justify massive deployment — it had over 80 GW of solar PV installed by end of 2023 and regularly generates large fractions of its electricity from solar.

Wind turbine noise is a common concern in permitting disputes, but modern turbines are typically inaudible beyond about 500 metres. The dominant sound is a 'swishing' from aerodynamic turbulence at the blade tips, which has been reduced by serrated trailing edge designs inspired by the silent feathers of owls.

China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) financed over $50 billion in overseas energy projects between 2014 and 2020, predominantly in coal power. Under international pressure, China announced in 2021 it would stop financing new coal power plants abroad, a major shift affecting dozens of planned projects in developing countries.

A thermal power plant's 'heat rate' measures fuel efficiency in BTUs required to generate one kWh of electricity. The lower the heat rate, the more efficient the plant — modern gas combined cycle plants achieve heat rates near 6,000 BTU/kWh, while old coal plants can exceed 12,000 BTU/kWh.

The Photovoltaic Effect — the process by which light photons knock electrons loose from a material to generate an electric current — was first observed by Edmond Becquerel in 1839 when he was just 19 years old. It would take over a century before Bell Labs turned the discovery into a practical device.

The global electricity sector is on track to be the most rapidly decarbonizing sector of the energy system, with clean electricity projected to rise from 39% of global electricity in 2023 to over 60% by 2030 under announced policies. This is primarily driven by the record pace of solar and wind deployment.

The world's highest-altitude commercial wind farm is located in the Tibetan Plateau in China, where turbines operate above 4,500 metres. At such elevations, air is roughly 60% as dense as at sea level, reducing wind energy yield — manufacturers develop specially designed low-density-air turbines with longer blades to compensate.

Energy storage mandates in California, passed through AB 2514, required the state's investor-owned utilities to procure 1,325 MW of energy storage by 2020. California now mandates that new homes include solar panels and is moving toward all-electric building codes.

The levelized cost of offshore wind dropped 60% between 2010 and 2022 — from roughly $330/MWh to around $92/MWh globally — driven by turbine scale-up, competitive auctions, and supply chain maturation. Some recent European auctions have achieved prices as low as $50/MWh.

The Breakthrough Energy Sciences initiative funds basic research on materials for energy — new electrocatalysts, battery chemistries, superconductors, and membranes — recognizing that many next-generation clean energy technologies depend on discoveries not yet made. It was founded by Bill Gates and partners in 2016.

The Sabatier reaction converts CO₂ and hydrogen into methane and water, enabling synthetic natural gas (SNG) production using green hydrogen and captured CO₂. SNG can be injected directly into existing gas infrastructure, offering a path to decarbonize heating without replacing pipelines.

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) or Guarantees of Origin (GOs) are market instruments that certify that one megawatt-hour of electricity was generated from a renewable source, enabling corporations to claim renewable electricity use even when connected to mixed-source grids. Over 350 TWh of RECs are traded globally each year.

The RE100 initiative, launched in 2014, brings together over 400 major corporations — including Apple, Google, IKEA, BMW, and Unilever — that have committed to sourcing 100% of their electricity from renewables. Collectively they consume over 300 TWh of electricity per year.

Tanzania's Lake Kivu shares a remarkable natural resource with neighboring DRC: its deep waters contain approximately 60 km³ of dissolved methane generated by biological decomposition and volcanic activity. Rwanda's KivuWatt project harvests this methane to generate up to 25 MW of electricity.

Advanced nuclear reactors using Generation IV designs include molten salt, sodium-cooled fast, very high temperature, and gas-cooled reactors. These next-generation designs target higher safety (passive safety), better waste profiles, and potentially the ability to 'burn' existing spent nuclear fuel as fresh input.

The Atacama Desert's lithium triangle — spanning Chile, Bolivia, and Argentina — contains more than 50% of the world's lithium reserves. As demand for lithium-ion batteries surges with EV adoption, this region has become one of the world's most geopolitically contested resource zones.

The energy stored in the world's total installed lithium-ion battery capacity — across EVs, grid storage, and consumer electronics — surpassed 1 terawatt-hour (TWh) for the first time in 2022. For comparison, global electricity consumption is approximately 28,000 TWh per year.

Nigeria is Africa's largest oil producer yet experiences chronic electricity shortages, with only about 7,000 MW of operational generation for 220 million people — equivalent to Houston, Texas. This 'resource curse' paradox illustrates why oil wealth does not automatically translate into energy access.

The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster of March 2011, triggered by the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami, led Japan to shut down all 54 of its nuclear reactors — which had supplied about 30% of Japan's electricity. Japan subsequently increased LNG imports massively, contributing to higher global gas prices.

Wind energy was used mechanically for grinding grain and pumping water for over 2,000 years before electricity was harnessed. Persia's early vertical-axis wind mills date to the 7th century CE, and the familiar European horizontal-axis post mill appeared in the 12th century.

Net metering allows homeowners with rooftop solar to receive a credit on their electricity bill for surplus power exported to the grid, priced at the retail electricity rate. It has been a powerful driver of rooftop solar adoption in the U.S. but is increasingly being reformed as solar penetration raises equity and cost-recovery concerns.

Cobalt, crucial for many lithium-ion cathode chemistries, is primarily mined in the Democratic Republic of Congo, which holds about 70% of global reserves. Concerns over child labor in artisanal cobalt mining and supply chain concentration have driven major battery companies to develop cobalt-free or cobalt-reduced cathode formulations.

Spent nuclear fuel from reactors is first stored in large pools of water at reactor sites to cool for several years, then optionally moved to dry cask storage — sealed steel and concrete containers. High-level nuclear waste remains hazardous for tens of thousands of years, and no country yet has an operating permanent deep geological repository.

Finland's Onkalo spent nuclear fuel repository, currently under construction deep in granite bedrock, will be the world's first permanent disposal site for high-level nuclear waste. It is designed to safely contain spent fuel for 100,000 years without requiring any active monitoring.

Power purchase agreements (PPAs) are long-term contracts between energy buyers (utilities or corporations) and renewable energy developers, providing price certainty that enables financing of new projects. Corporate PPAs for renewable energy grew from less than 1 GW globally in 2013 to over 50 GW in 2022.

The concept of district cooling — centrally chilling water and distributing it via insulated pipes to cool buildings — is the thermal equivalent of district heating and is especially valuable in hot Middle Eastern cities. Dubai operates one of the world's largest district cooling networks, serving hundreds of commercial buildings.

Low-emissivity (low-e) window coatings apply a microscopically thin metallic layer to glass that reflects infrared heat while allowing visible light to pass through — reducing winter heat loss by up to 50% compared to ordinary glass. They are now standard in most new building construction in cold climates.

South Korea's K-STAR tokamak set a new world record in 2023 by maintaining a plasma temperature of 100 million degrees Celsius for 48 seconds — surpassing its previous record of 30 seconds. This feat demonstrates progress toward the sustained plasma conditions required for a practical fusion power plant.

Synthetic inertia — software-based emulation of the flywheel effect of spinning generators — is being implemented in grid-scale inverters to stabilize frequency on high-renewable grids. The development of grid-forming inverters, which actively control voltage and frequency rather than following the grid, is considered a breakthrough for 100% renewable electricity systems.

The world's longest submarine power cable is the NorNed cable linking Norway and the Netherlands over 580 km of North Sea floor, enabling Norway to export surplus hydropower to the Netherlands and import wind power when demand exceeds Norwegian generation capacity.

Perovskite-silicon tandem solar cells layer a perovskite cell on top of a silicon cell, capturing different parts of the solar spectrum to exceed the Shockley-Queisser limit for single-junction cells. Longi Green Energy and KAUST achieved a certified tandem efficiency of 33.9% in 2023 — the highest ever recorded for a two-terminal tandem.

Electrification of home heating through heat pumps could cut global CO₂ emissions by up to 1.5 billion tonnes per year by 2050, according to the IEA — equivalent to the current annual emissions of all of Russia. Heat pump adoption is accelerating in Europe, the U.S., and China as governments incentivize fossil fuel boiler replacements.

Concentrating Solar Power (CSP) plants use an area of mirrors called a 'solar field' that can span several square kilometers. The world's largest CSP project is Morocco's Noor Complex, but the largest planned is Saudi Arabia's NEOM solar project, which envisions gigawatts of CSP to provide round-the-clock renewable power.

The Sundarbans mangrove forest, shared by India and Bangladesh, is both threatened by and a potential solution to climate change: mangroves sequester carbon at up to five times the rate of tropical forests per hectare. Protecting and restoring coastal mangroves is being promoted as a 'blue carbon' climate strategy.

The first photovoltaic satellite — Vanguard 1, launched in 1958 — used solar cells to power its radio transmitter and became the oldest man-made object still in orbit. Solar power has since become standard for almost all satellites.

Hydrogen embrittlement — the absorption of hydrogen atoms into metal, making it brittle and prone to cracking — is a key materials challenge for hydrogen infrastructure. Pipelines, valves, and compressors must use specially selected alloys or coatings to handle high-pressure hydrogen safely.

Electrified aviation is advancing rapidly at the small aircraft level: Eviation's Alice electric plane completed its first flight in 2022 and Pipistrel's Alpha Electro is already FAA-certified for flight training. But full electrification of long-haul aviation awaits radical battery breakthroughs or shifts to hydrogen or SAF.

The Ogallala Aquifer, one of the world's largest underground water reserves, stretches beneath eight U.S. Great Plains states and irrigates about 30% of all groundwater-irrigated cropland in the U.S. — much of it used for growing biofuel corn. Its depletion by irrigation is an intersecting water-energy-food nexus challenge.

The world's largest battery storage project (as of 2024) is Vistra's Moss Landing Energy Storage Facility in California, with 750 MW / 3,000 MWh of lithium-ion battery capacity. At full discharge, it can power approximately 225,000 homes for four hours.

Tidal Lagoon Power proposed building enclosed tidal lagoons — giant sea walls in shallow coastal areas — to capture tidal rise and fall through turbines. The Swansea Bay Tidal Lagoon in Wales was proposed as the world's first commercial tidal lagoon but was rejected by the UK government in 2018 over cost concerns.

The Cobb-Douglas production function in economics treats energy as a factor of production alongside labor and capital, and research shows that energy access is strongly correlated with economic development. Countries that have expanded electricity access consistently show improvements in health, education, and GDP per capita.

Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS) grows biomass that absorbs CO₂ from the atmosphere, burns it for energy, and captures and stores the resulting emissions underground — theoretically resulting in net negative carbon emissions. Most IPCC climate models rely heavily on BECCS but critics question the land and water requirements.

Texas produces more wind power than any other U.S. state, generating over 130 TWh of wind electricity in 2023 — more than any other state and more than most countries. West Texas and the Panhandle contain some of the best wind resources in the United States.

The 'prosumer' — a portmanteau of producer and consumer — describes households or businesses that both produce (via rooftop solar or other DERs) and consume electricity. Prosumers are legally recognized in EU energy regulations and can sell surplus energy to the grid or neighbors through local energy communities.

The world's deepest geothermal borehole was drilled in Kola, Russia in 1989 — the Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12.26 km, encountering temperatures over 180°C. While drilled for scientific purposes, deep drilling technology is being adapted for enhanced geothermal systems targeting high temperatures at great depth.

The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) found that energy infrastructure — particularly dams, transmission lines, wind farms, and mining for critical minerals — poses growing threats to biodiversity. Careful siting and integrated environmental planning are essential for a just energy transition.

Grid parity — the point at which the cost of generating electricity from a renewable source equals or falls below the retail price of electricity from the grid — was achieved by rooftop solar PV in many sunny countries by around 2014–2017. Today, utility-scale renewables have achieved grid parity in almost every country on Earth.

The British Thermal Unit (BTU) — the amount of energy needed to raise one pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit — is still widely used in the U.S. energy industry, while most of the world uses joules or kilowatt-hours. One BTU equals approximately 1,055 joules or 0.000293 kWh.

The Giga-factory model, pioneered by Tesla at its Nevada battery plant, applies high-volume automotive manufacturing techniques to battery production, driving down costs through scale, automation, and vertical integration. Globally, over 300 gigafactories producing batteries for EVs and storage are planned or under construction as of 2024.

The 2022 global heat pump market saw sales of 13 million units, with China the largest market. A heat pump achieves a coefficient of performance (COP) of 3–5, meaning it delivers 3–5 units of heat for every unit of electricity consumed — making it dramatically more efficient than electric resistance heating (COP = 1).

Vaclav Smil, one of the most cited scholars on energy systems, emphasizes that energy transitions are historically very slow — spanning 50–70 years — because they involve replacing vast stocks of capital equipment (power plants, pipelines, vehicles, buildings). He cautions against assuming current decarbonization timelines are achievable.

Solar PV panels work by the photovoltaic effect: photons from sunlight excite electrons in a semiconductor (usually silicon) across its band gap, creating a flow of current. Modern commercial silicon panels consist of multiple individual cells wired in series and parallel to produce useful voltages and currents.

The Western European power grid ('the continental synchronous area') operates at a precisely maintained frequency of 50 Hz — a deviation of more than ±200 mHz can trigger automatic load-shedding or generator trip. As coal and nuclear plants retire, maintaining this frequency with inverter-based renewables is a major grid engineering challenge.

The electricity sector accounts for about 25% of global greenhouse gas emissions — second only to the industry sector (including cement, steel, and chemicals). The power sector is typically decarbonized first in most climate scenarios because it has the most commercially mature zero-carbon solutions.

Offshore wind development in the United States was slow to begin — the country had no operating offshore wind for decades despite strong resources — but is now accelerating, with the 800 MW Vineyard Wind (Massachusetts) being the first major commercial project to enter construction in 2023.

Hydroelectric reservoirs can also emit significant quantities of methane and CO₂ from decomposition of flooded vegetation, particularly in tropical regions. Brazil's Balbina reservoir, built in the Amazon basin in 1987, has been found to emit more greenhouse gases than an equivalent coal power plant.

Onshore wind and solar PV now make up the two largest sources of new electricity generation capacity added globally every year. In 2023, solar alone exceeded additions from all fossil fuels combined for the first time in history.

The global capacity of floating offshore wind is projected to reach 250 GW by 2050, largely unlocking deep-water wind resources off the coasts of Japan, South Korea, Norway, California, and the US East Coast where fixed-bottom foundations are impractical. Floating wind LCOE is expected to converge with fixed-bottom by 2035.

Advanced metering infrastructure (AMI) — 'smart meters' — send real-time electricity consumption data to utilities, enabling time-of-use pricing, remote disconnection, and automated outage detection. The U.S. had over 115 million smart meters installed by end of 2022, covering about 80% of all U.S. electricity customers.

The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant in Ukraine, with six reactors and 5.7 GW of capacity, is the largest nuclear power plant in Europe. Its occupation by Russian forces during the 2022 invasion caused global nuclear safety alarms, with IAEA teams deployed to monitor the site.

The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) of the Kyoto Protocol allowed developed countries to invest in emissions reduction projects in developing nations and receive carbon credits. Over 7,000 CDM projects were registered by 2020, though many were criticized for questionable additionality.

Solar-powered desalination plants can provide clean drinking water in water-scarce, solar-rich regions like the Middle East and North Africa, removing the need for fossil fuel-powered desalination. Saudi Arabia's NEOM project includes one of the world's largest solar-powered desalination facilities.

Low-income and minority communities in the United States are disproportionately exposed to air pollution from fossil fuel power plants — a phenomenon documented by the U.S. EPA as 'cumulative environmental burden.' The Justice40 Initiative directs 40% of federal clean energy and climate investments to disadvantaged communities.

The thermoelectric effect (Seebeck effect), discovered in 1821, generates electricity from a temperature gradient across dissimilar conductors. Radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) exploit this effect using the heat from radioactive decay to power deep-space probes like Voyager 1 and 2, still transmitting from beyond the solar system.

The Arctic has been warming roughly four times faster than the global average due to 'Arctic amplification' — a feedback loop where melting sea ice exposes dark ocean water that absorbs more heat. Melting permafrost releases stored methane, potentially creating a powerful climate tipping point.

source.name: National Snow and Ice Data Center

text: The global coal industry employs about 9 million people, primarily in China, India, Indonesia, and the United States. Just transition programs — which provide retraining, pension support, and economic diversification for coal workers and communities — are considered essential for politically viable clean energy transitions.

Rooftop solar potential in sub-Saharan Africa — where most electricity connections are expected in the coming decades — is enormous. A 2020 IRENA study estimated that Africa's theoretical rooftop solar potential is nearly 6,000 GW, more than 20 times the continent's current total installed electricity capacity.

The global mean surface energy imbalance — the excess energy Earth absorbs from the Sun compared to what it radiates to space due to greenhouse gases — is approximately 0.9 W/m². Though tiny, this imbalance drives all of global warming, and 90% of its cumulative heat is absorbed by the oceans.

Renewable energy now attracts more investment than fossil fuels each year: in 2023, clean energy investment globally reached $1.7 trillion — for the first time more than 1.7 times the $1 trillion invested in fossil fuels. This ratio is expected to widen further through the end of the decade.

The Haber-Bosch process, developed in 1909 by Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, uses high temperatures and pressures to synthesize ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen — underpinning the fertilizer that feeds roughly half the world's current population. It consumes about 2% of global energy and produces about 1.8% of global CO₂ emissions.

Deep geothermal energy via closed-loop systems — circulating a working fluid through pipes inserted into hot rock without requiring naturally permeable formations — could open up geothermal to virtually any location worldwide. Companies like Eavor Technologies in Canada are commercializing 'deep closed-loop' geothermal systems.

The Drax power station in the UK — once the largest coal plant in Europe — converted four of its six generating units to burn wood pellets imported mainly from the U.S. Southeast by 2015. Drax now claims to be one of Europe's largest renewable power generators, though the sustainability of its biomass fuel is heavily contested.

Stellarators have the potential advantage over tokamaks of steady-state operation — unlike tokamaks, they don't require a pulsed plasma current that limits operation time. Germany's Wendelstein 7-X experiment has demonstrated 30-minute plasma discharges and confirmed the theoretical advantages of the complex stellarator magnetic coil geometry.

source.name: Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics

text: The IEA's 'Electricity Market Report' found that global electricity demand growth is accelerating due to EV charging, data centers, AI, and electrification of heat. Global electricity demand is expected to grow 4% per year through 2026 — the fastest sustained growth since the 2000s.

The world's largest producer of wind turbines is Goldwind of China, followed by Vestas of Denmark, Siemens Gamesa of Spain/Germany, Envision of China, and GE Vernova of the United States. Chinese manufacturers dominate the domestic Chinese market while European and American manufacturers lead internationally.

Cellulosic ethanol is produced from agricultural residues, wood chips, and dedicated energy grasses like switchgrass — not food crops — addressing the 'food vs. fuel' debate around corn ethanol. Despite decades of R&D, cellulosic ethanol plants have struggled to achieve commercial viability at scale due to the difficulty and cost of breaking down lignocellulose.

Microreactors — nuclear fission reactors smaller than 10 MW electric — are being developed for remote community power, military bases, industrial heat, and even spacecraft propulsion. The U.S. Defense Department's 'Project Pele' is testing a transportable 1–5 MW microreactor that can be carried on a truck.

Global energy consumption is roughly divided into three roughly equal parts: industry (about 37%), transport (about 23%), and buildings and agriculture (about 25%), with the remainder in non-energy uses. This breakdown guides policy priorities — industry is the hardest sector to decarbonize.

The Meridian Energy's Lake Pukaki hydroelectric system in New Zealand is so large that it can vary generation by over 1,000 MW within minutes, acting as a giant 'battery' for the South Island grid. New Zealand generates about 80–90% of its electricity from renewables.

The global energy transition is estimated to require $4–5 trillion of annual investment by 2030, roughly four times the current level. About two-thirds of this investment needs to flow to developing and emerging economies, where financing costs are two to three times higher than in developed countries.

The 'rebound effect' (Jevons paradox) describes how improvements in energy efficiency can lead to increased overall consumption as lower costs spur greater use. Economist William Stanley Jevons first described this in 1865 with coal, and it remains a key consideration in energy efficiency policy design.

source.name: International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis

text: Submarine volcanic activity — which has been estimated to release CO₂ at a relatively steady rate — accounts for less than 1% of current global volcanic CO₂ emissions, which are themselves about 40 times smaller than human emissions from fossil fuels. The 'volcanoes are responsible' climate argument is not supported by scientific evidence.

Electric vehicle battery chemistries are diversifying: lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries — safer, cheaper, and longer-lasting but lower energy density — are dominating the Chinese market, while NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) batteries are preferred for premium long-range EVs in Western markets.

The Yucca Mountain nuclear waste repository in Nevada was the designated U.S. high-level nuclear waste site from 1987, but President Obama withdrew its license application in 2010 amid political opposition. The U.S. has spent over $15 billion on Yucca Mountain studies and still has no permanent solution for its 90,000 tonnes of spent nuclear fuel.

Underwater tidal kite systems — devices that 'fly' in tidal currents like a kite, sweeping large volumes of water through a small turbine at high speed — were pioneered by Sweden's Minesto. Their Deep Green technology is operational in the Faroe Islands and is designed for low-velocity tidal currents where conventional turbines are uneconomical.

The 'Green New Deal' resolution introduced in the U.S. Congress in 2019 by Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Ed Markey called for a 10-year national mobilization to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and create millions of clean energy jobs. While it didn't pass, it shaped subsequent climate legislation including the Inflation Reduction Act.

Gas turbine engines — derived from jet engine technology — are the workhorses of natural gas power generation. Modern advanced gas turbines achieve combined-cycle efficiencies over 63%, with the remaining thermal energy recovered from exhaust gases to generate additional steam power in a secondary Rankine cycle.

Thailand has one of Asia's most aggressive bioenergy programs, mandating bioethanol blending in petrol and biodiesel blending in diesel fuels. The country produces bioethanol mainly from cassava and sugarcane, and biodiesel from palm oil.

Energy independence has long been a stated goal of many nations, but true independence is rare: even renewable energy supply chains for solar panels, wind turbines, and batteries are globally interconnected. China manufactures over 95% of the world's solar polysilicon and about 80% of wind turbine permanent magnets.

Baseload power — electricity supply maintained continuously to meet the minimum level of consumer demand — was historically supplied by coal, nuclear, and large hydro plants running 24/7. With falling costs of storage, the concept of 'firm renewable power' is replacing the traditional baseload paradigm.

The 'green premium' — the extra cost of a zero-carbon alternative versus the incumbent fossil fuel technology — varies enormously by sector. It is already negative (renewables are cheaper) for electricity generation, is relatively modest for EVs and heat pumps, and remains very high for aviation, shipping, and industrial heat.

The Sun produces energy through the proton-proton chain reaction, where four hydrogen protons ultimately fuse to form one helium-4 nucleus, releasing approximately 26.7 MeV of energy per reaction. The Sun converts about 4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second via this process.

China's Beibu Gulf offshore wind zone in the South China Sea is being developed as one of the world's most productive marine renewable energy areas, with planned capacity exceeding 30 GW. The region benefits from steady monsoon winds and proximity to major industrial coastal cities.

Electricity wheeling allows industrial consumers to transmit their contracted renewable electricity across a third party's power grid, paying a wheeling charge. This mechanism enables large factories in countries like India and Brazil to source renewable power from distant farms without building private transmission lines.

Energy return on investment (EROI) for photovoltaic solar panels has improved dramatically over time: early panels in the 1970s had an EROI approaching 1:1, meaning they barely produced more energy than went into making them, while modern silicon panels have an EROI of approximately 10–30:1 depending on location.

The Ethiopian Grand Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile, nearing completion in the early 2020s with a 5,150 MW capacity, is Africa's largest hydroelectric project. It has caused significant diplomatic tensions with Egypt and Sudan, which depend on Nile water and fear the dam will reduce their share.

Electricity markets operate on multiple timescales simultaneously: spot markets (seconds to hours), day-ahead markets, capacity markets (years ahead), and long-term bilateral contracts. Price formation in these nested markets determines the economics of all generation investments.

Photovoltaic 'anti-soiling' coatings made from hydrophobic materials help rain clean dust and pollution from solar panels, which can otherwise reduce output by 20–40% in desert environments. In India and the Middle East, 'robotic cleaning' systems using dry brushes are increasingly used to maintain panel efficiency without water.

The 'virtual net metering' model extends net metering to shared community solar gardens, allowing customers who can't install rooftop panels (renters, apartment dwellers, shaded homes) to buy a share of a remote solar array and receive credits on their electricity bill. Over 40 U.S. states have enacted community solar programs.

The first large-scale lithium-ion grid battery — the Hornsdale Power Reserve, built by Tesla in South Australia in 100 days in 2017 — initially held 100 MW/129 MWh. It responded to grid emergencies in milliseconds, saving consumers millions in frequency regulation costs and demonstrating that batteries could replace 'peaker' gas plants.

The Severn Estuary in the UK has the second-highest tidal range in the world (up to 15 metres) and a proposed tidal barrage across it could generate up to 8.6 GW of electricity — about 5% of UK demand. Multiple economic and environmental studies have been conducted since the 1980s but no project has been approved.

Methane hydrates — solid ice-like structures trapping methane in deepwater sediments and permafrost — contain more carbon than all known coal, oil, and gas reserves combined. Japan and China have conducted offshore extraction tests, but commercial exploitation faces major technical, economic, and climate risk challenges.

The global average energy consumption per person is about 75 GJ/year, but this masks enormous inequality: the average American consumes roughly 300 GJ/year while the average sub-Saharan African consumes around 15 GJ/year. Achieving development-level energy access for all while decarbonizing is the central challenge of sustainable development.

The global uranium market is dominated by Kazakhstan (43% of production), Namibia, Canada, and Australia. Canada's Athabasca Basin hosts the world's highest-grade uranium deposits, with ore grades exceeding 20% U₃O₈ — over 100 times the global average mine grade.

The COP28 climate summit in Dubai in December 2023 produced the first-ever global agreement to 'transition away from fossil fuels.' It also tripled the global target for renewable energy capacity to 11,000 GW by 2030 and doubled the global target for energy efficiency improvements.

Tokamak Energy's ST40 spherical tokamak in Oxford reached a plasma temperature of 100 million degrees Celsius in 2022 — hotter than the Sun's core — making it the first privately funded fusion device to achieve that milestone. Spherical tokamaks use a tighter magnetic configuration that could lead to more compact, cheaper fusion reactors.

The 1973 oil crisis, the invention of the silicon solar cell in 1954, Edison's first power station in 1882, Becquerel's discovery of the photovoltaic effect in 1839, Watt's steam engine patent in 1769, and the NIF fusion ignition in 2022 represent a through-line of energy history: each pivotal moment reshaped how civilization powers itself. The global energy system is now in the midst of its most rapid and consequential transformation since the Industrial Revolution.

The world's first commercial offshore wind farm, Vindeby, was built off the coast of Denmark in 1991 with just 11 turbines and 4.95 MW of capacity. Today, single offshore wind turbines can exceed 15 MW each, demonstrating a 300-fold increase in individual turbine size over three decades.

Perovskite solar cells, named after the mineral with the same crystal structure, have seen their laboratory efficiency jump from 3.8% in 2009 to over 26% by 2024 — one of the fastest efficiency improvements of any photovoltaic technology. Their low-cost manufacturing potential could make solar electricity even cheaper than silicon panels.

China installed more solar power capacity in 2023 alone than the entire world installed cumulatively through 2022. This staggering pace of deployment has made China home to over 40% of global solar manufacturing capacity and the leading force in the global energy transition.

The Itaipu Dam on the Brazil-Paraguay border was the world's largest hydroelectric plant by annual generation for many years, producing about 103 TWh of electricity in its record year of 2016. Paraguay sells most of its share of Itaipu's output to Brazil, making hydroelectric exports a major portion of Paraguay's national income.

Thermal energy storage using molten salt allows concentrating solar power plants to generate electricity for up to 15 hours after sunset. The Crescent Dunes plant in Nevada was among the first to operate entirely on stored heat after dark, demonstrating that solar energy can be dispatchable around the clock.

Norway generates over 90% of its electricity from hydropower and is one of the world's largest exporters of both oil and natural gas. This paradox allows Norwegians to enjoy cheap, clean domestic electricity while profiting from fossil fuel exports, funding a sovereign wealth fund now worth over $1.7 trillion.

The 'duck curve' is a graph of electricity demand minus solar generation throughout the day that resembles a duck — showing a deep midday trough when solar is abundant and a steep evening ramp when solar drops and demand peaks. California grid operators coined the term and it has become a central challenge for managing high-solar grids.

Geothermal energy provides about 30% of Iceland's electricity and over 66% of its total primary energy supply when including direct heat use for space heating. Iceland sits atop the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, giving it access to geothermal resources that allow it to run its economy almost entirely on renewable energy.

The world's largest wind turbine as of 2024 is the Siemens Gamesa SG 14-236 DD, with a rotor diameter of 236 meters — larger than the Eiffel Tower is tall. A single rotation of its blades sweeps an area greater than 13 football fields.

Energy poverty affects approximately 770 million people worldwide who lack access to electricity, mostly in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The IEA estimates that universal energy access by 2030 would require only a 0.2% increase in global energy-related CO₂ emissions, showing that equity and climate goals are not fundamentally in conflict.

Pumped-storage hydropower represents over 90% of all grid-scale electricity storage capacity worldwide, with about 160 GW installed globally. Water is pumped uphill when electricity is cheap and released through turbines when demand peaks, acting as a giant rechargeable battery for the grid.

The U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, stored in underground salt caverns along the Gulf of Mexico, holds up to 714 million barrels of crude oil — the largest emergency petroleum stockpile in the world. The salt caverns were chosen because their natural impermeability makes them ideal low-cost, leak-proof storage vessels.

Direct air capture (DAC) technology removes CO₂ directly from the atmosphere using chemical reactions, but currently costs $400–$1,000 per tonne of CO₂ removed — far above the $50–$100 needed for large-scale deployment. The world's largest DAC plant, Mammoth in Iceland, can capture 36,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year, a tiny fraction of global emissions of 37 billion tonnes.

The Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster in 2011 caused Japan to shut down all of its 54 nuclear reactors, forcing the country to increase fossil fuel imports dramatically. Japanese electricity prices approximately doubled in the years following, and the country's CO₂ emissions rose by about 50 million tonnes annually.

The world's first nuclear-powered submarine, the USS Nautilus, traveled over 62,000 nautical miles in its first two years of operation without refueling. Nuclear propulsion freed submarines from the need to surface regularly to recharge batteries, revolutionizing naval warfare.

source.name: U.S. Naval History and Heritage Command

text: Green hydrogen produced via electrolysis powered by renewable electricity could theoretically decarbonize industries that are hard to electrify directly, including steel, cement, shipping, and aviation. However, the process is only about 70% efficient, making green hydrogen more expensive than direct electrification for most applications.

The Atacama Desert in Chile receives more solar radiation per square meter than almost any other place on Earth, making it the world's most productive location for solar energy generation per panel installed. Some Chilean solar projects have bid electricity at under $0.02 per kWh — among the lowest prices ever recorded for any energy source.

High-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission lines can carry electricity over thousands of kilometers with losses as low as 3% per 1,000 km, compared to 6–8% for conventional AC lines. China operates the world's longest HVDC line — the ±1,100 kV Zhundong-Wannan link stretching 3,324 km across the country.

The Deepwater Horizon oil spill in 2010 released approximately 4.9 million barrels of crude oil into the Gulf of Mexico over 87 days, making it the largest accidental marine oil spill in history. The disaster resulted in $65 billion in costs for BP and spurred major regulatory changes for deepwater drilling.

An electric vehicle's drivetrain converts about 85–90% of battery energy into motion, compared to only 20–40% for internal combustion engines. This fundamental efficiency advantage means EVs require roughly one-third the energy per kilometer traveled, dramatically reducing lifetime energy costs even when charged from fossil-fuel power plants.

The Larderello geothermal field in Tuscany, Italy has been producing electricity since 1904, making it the world's oldest geothermal power station still in operation. It currently generates about 600 MW, providing around 2% of Italy's electricity and heating thousands of local homes.

Coal was responsible for about 36% of global electricity generation in 2023, despite being the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel. China, which burns more coal than all other countries combined, accounts for roughly 54% of global coal power generation.

The 'energy return on investment' (EROI) measures how much energy is produced for every unit expended in extraction. Oil fields in the early 20th century had EROIs of 100:1, while modern unconventional oil (tar sands, shale) has an EROI of roughly 3:1 to 10:1, meaning more energy is 'spent' obtaining each barrel.

Brazil produces more than 80% of its electricity from renewable sources, primarily hydropower but increasingly wind and solar. Brazil's ethanol program, launched after the 1973 oil crisis, means that around 40% of Brazilian fuel demand is met by sugarcane-based biofuel — the world's most efficient large-scale biofuel program.

Grid-scale vanadium redox flow batteries store energy in liquid vanadium electrolyte tanks, allowing energy capacity to be scaled simply by increasing tank size. They can charge and discharge simultaneously, have lifespans exceeding 20 years, and do not degrade with cycling — advantages over lithium-ion for long-duration storage.

The Trans-Alaska Pipeline System (TAPS) stretches 800 miles from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez through some of the world's most extreme terrain. Built in 1977, it has carried over 18 billion barrels of oil and was engineered to withstand temperatures from -80°F to +95°F and an 8.5-magnitude earthquake.

Floating solar panels (floatovoltaics) installed on reservoirs and lakes offer a dual benefit: they generate electricity while reducing water evaporation by up to 70% by shading the surface. A 2021 study estimated that covering just 10% of the world's man-made reservoirs with floatovoltaics could meet global electricity demand.

The U.S. electricity grid is actually three separate, mostly non-interconnected grids: the Eastern Interconnection, the Western Interconnection, and the Texas Interconnection (ERCOT). Texas runs its own isolated grid partly to avoid federal regulation, a decision that contributed to catastrophic failures during the 2021 winter storm.

Compressed air energy storage (CAES) works by pumping air into underground caverns during low-demand periods and releasing it through turbines when demand is high. The McIntosh CAES plant in Alabama has operated since 1991, storing air in a natural salt cavern at pressures up to 1,000 psi.

The Rance Tidal Power Station in Brittany, France, opened in 1966 and was the world's first tidal power plant. With 24 turbines and 240 MW capacity, it has been producing electricity for over 50 years and generates about 600 GWh annually — enough for roughly 130,000 homes.

The 'levelized cost of electricity' (LCOE) accounts for all costs of a power plant over its lifetime divided by total electricity produced, enabling apples-to-apples comparison across technologies. By 2023, utility-scale solar and onshore wind had LCOEs below $50/MWh in most markets, cheaper than new coal or gas plants almost everywhere.
