text: The 'thermoelectric effect' discovered by Thomas Johann Seebeck in 1821 produces a voltage when two different conductors are joined at junctions held at different temperatures. Modern thermoelectric devices using bismuth telluride achieve efficiency around 5–8% — far below Carnot limits — but their solid-state reliability makes them ideal for niche applications like remote power and waste heat recovery.

Portugal achieved 100% renewable electricity generation on an annual basis in 2024 — the first large country in Europe to reach this milestone. Hydropower provides the backbone, with wind, solar, and geothermal completing the portfolio. In some months, Portugal exported surplus renewable electricity to Spain and France.

The 'Iodine-131 thyroid cancer' tragedy from the Chernobyl explosion resulted in over 6,000 cases of thyroid cancer, primarily in people who were children in 1986 and drank contaminated milk. This was largely preventable: distribution of potassium iodide tablets immediately after the accident would have blocked radioactive iodine absorption in the thyroid.

The 'energy-water-food nexus' recognizes that energy, water, and food production are deeply interdependent: agriculture uses 70% of global freshwater and 30% of global energy, energy production requires large amounts of water for cooling, and food waste accounts for about 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions. Addressing any one challenge requires considering all three.

The 'photovoltaic effect on the Moon' is being explored for lunar solar power stations that could beam energy to Earth or power future lunar bases. The Moon's lack of atmosphere means solar panels receive 30% more energy than on Earth's surface and are never blocked by clouds, but the 14-day lunar night requires enormous storage or a global lunar power grid.

The 'carbon offset market' allows companies to compensate for their emissions by funding projects that reduce CO₂ elsewhere, such as reforestation, renewable energy, or cookstove distribution. By 2023, the voluntary carbon market had grown to $2 billion but faced mounting criticism for poor quality credits, with some forest offset programs shown to have dramatically overstated carbon sequestration.

The 'photovoltaic thermal hybrid collector' (PVT) generates both electricity and heat from the same panel by using water circulation to cool the PV cells while collecting the heat for domestic hot water. PVT panels are about 20% more efficient than separate PV and thermal panels occupying the same roof area, making them attractive for space-constrained installations.

Wind turbines on land typically need wind speeds of at least 3 m/s to start generating and reach full output around 12–14 m/s; above 25 m/s they are shut down to prevent damage. The 'cut-in' and 'cut-out' wind speed characteristics mean turbines can only generate for about 30–40% of hours in average wind locations.

The 'Tokamak Energy' private fusion company in Oxford demonstrated plasma temperatures of 100 million°C in 2022, hotter than the Sun's core, in a compact spherical tokamak. Their business model aims to build a 150 MW commercial fusion plant by 2030, targeting electricity costs below $50/MWh — a tight but not impossible timeline according to independent fusion experts.

The 'Global Warming of 1.5°C' special report by the IPCC in 2018 found that limiting warming to 1.5°C instead of 2°C would prevent the displacement of 10 million people from coastal flooding, avoid the loss of virtually all tropical coral reefs, and reduce by half the share of Earth's surface affected by severe heat stress. These findings gave new urgency to the 1.5°C target.

The 'energy transition jobs' created in manufacturing clean energy equipment have been concentrated in Asia — particularly China, where most solar panels, batteries, and wind turbines are manufactured. Efforts by the U.S. IRA and EU to incentivize domestic manufacturing aim to diversify this supply chain and create local clean energy employment.

The Amazon rainforest is the world's largest terrestrial carbon sink, absorbing an estimated 2 billion tonnes of CO₂ per year. However, extensive deforestation has degraded some parts of the Amazon to the point where they now emit more carbon than they absorb — a watershed moment with profound implications for global climate stabilization.

The 'thorium fuel cycle' uses thorium-232, which is about three times more abundant than uranium in Earth's crust, as a fertile material that can be transmuted in reactors into uranium-233 for fuel. India, which has large thorium reserves but modest uranium deposits, has pursued thorium reactor development for decades, aiming for a three-stage nuclear program culminating in thorium-based reactors.

The 'Kelvin temperature scale' defines absolute zero as -273.15°C — the temperature at which atomic motion theoretically ceases. All thermodynamic efficiency calculations reference this absolute scale: the Carnot efficiency equation uses absolute temperatures, which is why high-temperature heat sources like nuclear and concentrated solar are inherently more valuable than low-temperature sources.

The 'Enel Green Power' subsidiary of Italy's Enel utility is one of the world's largest renewable energy companies, operating over 60 GW of renewable capacity across 30 countries. Enel's global strategy of developing solar, wind, geothermal, and hydro projects while divesting from coal has made it one of the most successful examples of a legacy utility's clean energy transition.

The 'energy price volatility' of fossil fuels is a fundamental disadvantage compared to renewables, whose 'fuel' is free. Oil prices have swung from $10 to $150 per barrel within the span of a few years multiple times since 1990, causing economic shocks that fall disproportionately on oil-importing developing countries.

The 'tipping point' for electric vehicle adoption appears to be around 5% market share, after which sales accelerate rapidly due to network effects from charging infrastructure, reduced range anxiety, and manufacturer commitment. Norway, the global EV leader, crossed this threshold around 2014; by 2023, EVs accounted for 82% of new car sales there.

The 'energy storage gap' between what is needed for a 100% renewable grid and what currently exists is enormous: the world needs about 10 TWh of storage to achieve 100% renewable electricity, but only has about 1 TWh today. Filling this gap requires storage equivalent to about 10,000 Hoover Dams — a scale of infrastructure investment unprecedented in energy history.

The 'solar-powered irrigation' revolution is transforming agriculture in India and sub-Saharan Africa, where cheap solar panels now power water pumps that previously ran on diesel. India has installed over 4 million solar irrigation pumps, reducing farmers' fuel costs dramatically — though the systems also raise concerns about unsustainable groundwater extraction.

The 'Doomsday Clock' maintained by the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists — which measures how close humanity is to existential catastrophe — added climate change as a second major threat alongside nuclear war in 2007. By 2023, it stood at 90 seconds to midnight — the closest it has ever been — reflecting combined risks from climate change, nuclear weapons, and disruptive technologies.

The 'energy transition' in transportation is advancing on multiple fronts simultaneously: electric passenger cars, electric two-wheelers, electric buses, electric rail, and hydrogen trucks. Bloomberg projects that EVs will represent 75% of new car sales globally by 2035, displacing over 20 million barrels per day of oil demand and eliminating a billion tonnes of CO₂ annually.

The 'wind-to-hydrogen' economics improve dramatically with access to high-quality wind resources: the North Sea has average wind speeds of 9–11 m/s, producing wind power at capacity factors of 50–60% and enabling green hydrogen at potentially $1–2/kg by the 2030s. At that price, green hydrogen could displace fossil fuels across multiple sectors.

The 'climate emergency' declarations by over 2,000 governments and subnational jurisdictions worldwide since 2016 have been criticized for rarely translating into binding emissions reductions. However, jurisdictions that declared climate emergencies have shown measurably faster clean energy adoption, suggesting the declarations influence investment and regulatory decisions even without legal force.

The 'fuel cell electric bus' is achieving commercial scale in China, which deployed over 5,000 fuel cell buses by 2023 — more than the rest of the world combined. Hydrogen buses offer longer range and faster refueling than battery buses for high-utilization urban routes, making them particularly attractive for bus rapid transit systems.

The 'oil spill microbes' discovered after the Deepwater Horizon disaster include naturally occurring bacteria and fungi that can metabolize hydrocarbons. The microbial community in the Gulf of Mexico degraded a significant fraction of the spilled oil within months, but some of the most toxic compounds — polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — persisted for years in seafloor sediments.

The 'solar eclipse effect' on electricity grids provides a controlled experiment in how the grid handles rapid changes in solar generation: during a total eclipse, solar output can drop from hundreds of GW to near zero in minutes, then recover just as quickly. European grid operators have successfully managed multiple total solar eclipses with careful advance planning.

The 'thermal mass' of buildings — the ability of walls, floors, and ceilings to absorb and store heat — can significantly reduce energy needed for heating and cooling. Traditional Mediterranean buildings used thick stone walls to stay cool in summer and warm in winter; modern passive buildings incorporate phase-change materials (PCMs) that can store 10 times more heat per kg than concrete.

The 'floating wind hub' concept for the North Sea envisions building an artificial energy island that would serve as both an offshore substation and a green hydrogen production facility. The Danish island-like platform would host hundreds of cable connections from surrounding wind farms and export both electricity and hydrogen to multiple countries simultaneously.

The 'energy transition in emerging markets' is different from developed country transitions: many countries in Asia and Africa are building new energy infrastructure for the first time and can 'leapfrog' to clean energy just as they leapfrogged fixed-line telephone infrastructure with mobile phones. Bangladesh increased its solar home system installations from 50,000 in 2003 to 5.5 million by 2018.

The 'global warming commitment' — the additional warming already locked in from past emissions even if we stopped emitting today — is estimated at about 0.3°C above current temperatures. This means that even if all emissions stopped immediately, the world would still warm further, and some impacts of climate change are now unavoidable regardless of future action.

The 'high-altitude wind energy' concept proposes using kites or tethered aircraft at altitudes of 1–10 km, where winds are stronger and more consistent than near the ground. Companies like Makani Power (later acquired by Google X and then disbanded) have demonstrated flying wind turbines, but the complexity of managing airspace and tether systems has prevented commercial scale.

The 'nuclear plant construction time' has diverged dramatically between East and West: China builds new nuclear plants in 5–6 years for $3–4 billion per GW, while Western plants like Hinkley Point C in the UK and Vogtle in the U.S. have taken 12–16 years and cost $15–35 billion per GW. This cost divergence has made nuclear energy economically challenging in Western markets.

The 'HVDC grid' in Europe, envisioned as the backbone of a pan-European clean energy system, would require burying cable or building submarine connections across multiple countries. Onshore HVDC lines face planning and permission challenges in densely populated Europe, making the underground or submarine routing more practical but significantly more expensive.

The 'clean cooking' challenge is not just a fuel switch but also a behavioral and cultural shift: many households in developing countries prefer the taste of food cooked over open fire and use cookstoves for lighting, warmth, and social gathering as well as cooking. Successful clean cooking transitions require stove designs that meet cultural preferences, not just technical efficiency targets.

The 'second law of thermodynamics' states that entropy — the disorder or randomness in a system — always increases in isolated systems. In practical energy terms, this means every energy conversion produces waste heat that cannot be recovered, and it is fundamentally impossible to build a perpetual motion machine or convert heat entirely to work without a temperature difference.

The 'hydrogen-iron ore' direct reduction process produces iron using hydrogen instead of coke, with steam as the only byproduct instead of CO₂. SSAB's HYBRIT project produced the world's first hydrogen-reduced iron in 2021, with delivery of the first hydrogen-based steel to Volvo for automotive use. Scaling this process requires vast amounts of green hydrogen.

The 'energy efficiency standard' for LED light bulbs, now mandated in most developed countries, has reduced lighting energy consumption by 75–80% compared to incandescent bulbs while providing better-quality light. Worldwide adoption of LEDs has saved an estimated 570 TWh of electricity annually — equivalent to shutting down 150 coal power plants.

The energy transition underway in the 21st century — from fossil fuels to renewable electricity, hydrogen, and electrification — represents the third great energy transition in human history, following the shift from biomass to coal in the 18th–19th centuries and the rise of oil and gas in the 20th century. Unlike previous transitions driven by resource abundance, this one is driven by necessity: the recognition that the climate system has finite capacity to absorb the consequences of burning fossil fuels, and that the alternatives have become cheaper than the fuels they replace.
